k76.name: Art as Environment - A Cultural Action at Plum Tree Creek
k76.creator: Wu Mali + Bamboo Curtain Studio
k76.place: Around Zhuwei, Tamsui, New Taipei; the Plum Tree Creek watershed
k76.year: 2010-2012 (2013 grand prize, visual arts, 11th Taishin Arts Award)
k76.summary:
The Shumeikeng Creek environmental art action is a long-term project planned in 2010–2012 by Wu Mali and the Zhuwei Art Studio, funded by the National Culture and Arts Foundation’s visual-arts curatorial programme, and winner of the grand prize in visual arts at the 11th Taishin Arts Award in 2013. It proposes “linking fragmented land with water”, strung along the roughly ten-kilometre Shumeikeng Creek to connect seemingly unrelated places — woodland, pig farms, high-rises and an MRT station.

It is not traditional photography or painting but is composed of several cultural actions — the Shumeikeng Creek Breakfast Club, the Village Shapes mobile museum, community theatre, Local Green Life (“Dyeing with Plants”), “A River in Front of My School Gate” and Water Dance (Lü’s study records five sub-projects, Taishin’s source six; this platform uses six) — carried out with local school teachers and students, residents and government departments.

Wu argues that “art plays not the role of beautification but the medium that triggers, connects and thinks”, placing herself as a weaver of relations. The location is marked as the Zhuwei area of Tamsui, New Taipei, according to the studio’s base and the creek’s position.
k76.selfDesc: Lu Pei-yi's study lists it under 'art as a method of social change', as a 2010 NCAF curatorial-project grant with five sub-projects (Breakfast Meeting, mobile museum, dyeing with plants, a creek in front of my school, community theatre), quoting Wu Mali that 'art is not a beautifier but a medium that triggers, connects and makes one think'. ArtEmperor (via ETtoday, 2013-05-23) notes the work by Wu Mali and Bamboo Curtain Studio won the grand prize in the visual arts category of the 11th Taishin Arts Award on 2013-05-11, proposing 'connecting fragmented land through water', a c.10-km creek linking hills, pig pens, high-rises and an MRT station, made of six cultural actions (Breakfast Meeting, Village Shape mobile museum, community theatre, local green living - dyeing with plants, A River in Front of My School, Water Dance), working with local schools, residents and government.
k76.editNote: Among the ten artists in Lu Pei-yi's study. The number of sub-projects differs slightly: Lu lists five, ArtEmperor six (adding 'Water Dance' and 'Village Shape'); the platform uses the fuller six and notes Lu's five. Location: Bamboo Curtain Studio is in Zhuwei, Tamsui, New Taipei, through which the creek runs, so 'city' is New Taipei; neither source spells out 'Zhuwei, New Taipei' verbatim, inferred from the studio and the creek. A strongly participatory case.
k76.pedagogicalInsight: The most borrowable thing is using a stream as a “thread”: seemingly scattered activities such as the breakfast club, theatre, plant dyeing and school lessons are strung into a whole by “water” and “the river basin”, bringing in residents, students and public offices. For courses on environmental education and community building, it shows how to make an ecological issue into a long-term, multi-site, cross-generation action rather than a one-off exhibition.
k76.why: Verified: Lu Pei-yi's study (academic) and the ArtEmperor report corroborate that it is Wu Mali and Bamboo Curtain Studio's long-term action, 'connecting fragmented land through water', made of several cultural actions, winning the grand prize in the visual arts category at the 11th Taishin Arts Award. Caveat: the sub-project count is given both ways (Lu five; ArtEmperor six); 'Zhuwei, New Taipei' is inferred from the studio and creek, not spelled out verbatim.

k77.name: New Paradise of Plants (Sa'owac community)
k77.creator: Hsu Su-chen, Lu Chien-ming
k77.place: The Sa'owac community on the bank of the Dahan River (an urban Amis self-build community, around Daxi, Taoyuan)
k77.year: 2008-2010 (grand prize, visual arts, 8th Taishin Arts Award)
k77.summary:
“Plant-Object New Paradise” is a long-term project (2008–2010) by Hsu Shu-chen and Lu Chien-ming at the Sawazi tribe by the Dahan River (a self-built Amis community that moved to the city, around Daxi, Taoyuan), which won the grand prize in visual arts at the 8th Taishin Arts Award. They combine ecological art with a cultural movement.

First they made botanical-specimen prints of the tribe’s farm plants; after the tribe was demolished they printed these images on T-shirts and marked members’ Amis names in romanisation, as a practice of “naming” and identity; then, through “Building a House: A Practice of the Social Contract”, they joined in self-built housing and even carried the display materials from their Kaohsiung Museum of Fine Arts exhibition back to the tribe as the foundation for building houses.

The project treats art as an alternative social movement, intervening directly in the tribe’s housing and survival; the two artists ask themselves “for whom does it create value? what are the effects inside the tribe (community) and outside in society?”. The jury called it “a model for Han Chinese participation in indigenous society”.
k77.selfDesc: Lu Pei-yi's study lists Hsu Su-chen and Lu Chien-ming under 'art as a method of social change', with New Paradise of Plants on the Dahan River bank at Sa'owac, fusing ecological art and cultural activism - botanical-specimen prints of farm plants, printed on T-shirts after demolition to 'name' residents, 'House-building: A Practice of Social Contract' self-build housing, and shipping the Kaohsiung museum's exhibition materials back as house foundations - and quoting their question 'value to whom? what effects inside the community and outside in society?'. The Taishin Arts Award page (2010-05-13) records the work winning the grand prize in the visual arts category of the 8th Taishin Arts Award, the jury calling it a 'hut-form work' made with the Amis, exploring living space and ways of life, 'establishing a model of Han participation in Indigenous society', around 'the material world of the riverside Amis'.
k77.editNote: Among the ten artists in Lu Pei-yi's study (Hsu Su-chen and Lu Chien-ming as a pair). Location: Sa'owac is on the Dahan River bank (around Daxi, Taoyuan), so 'city' is Taoyuan; Lu says only 'Sa'owac on the Dahan River bank' and the Taishin page only 'riverside Amis', neither spelling out the county, Taoyuan inferred from Sa'owac's location. The Taishin page's title misprints the artist's name; the body uses the correct form. Sa'owac, the prints and the shipped materials come mainly from Lu; Taishin independently confirms the award, the Amis collaboration and the housing theme.
k77.pedagogicalInsight: The most borrowable thing is connecting art directly to “the survival of dwelling”: not stopping at speaking for the tribe but going from botanical specimens and naming all the way to self-built houses, turning exhibition materials into a house foundation. For courses on indigenous peoples, land justice and urban-edge communities, it shows how art can become an “alternative social movement”, and presses the question the two artists asked themselves: for whom does it actually create value?
k77.why: Verified: Lu Pei-yi's study (academic) and the official Taishin Arts Award page corroborate that the work, by Hsu Su-chen and Lu Chien-ming with an Amis community, centres on housing/self-build and won the grand prize in the visual arts category at the 8th Taishin Arts Award. Caveat: Sa'owac, the Dahan River, the botanical prints and the shipped materials come from Lu; the county (Taoyuan) is inferred from Sa'owac's location, not spelled out in either source; the Taishin page misprints the artist's name in its title.

k74.name: TOA Lighting (Chou Yu-Cheng's exchange-platform works)
k74.creator: Chou Yu-Cheng
k74.place: Museum spaces including the Taipei Fine Arts Museum
k74.summary:
Chou Yu-cheng made a series of projects built on “the artist as an intermediary of resource flows”, of which “East Asia Lighting” (2010) is the signature work: he asked lighting companies to sponsor lamps to light a museum space that was originally empty — so the lamps acted as advertising for the companies, and after the exhibition the work was taken into the collection, answering the museum’s needs.

The work both lays open “the mechanisms of art production” and shows cooperation and exchange between art and the economy. Following the same line he also made “Take from Society, Use for Society” (2010, printing prints with grant money, selling them and donating the proceeds back to a foundation) and “Work History — Lu Chieh-te” (2012, working with temporary worker Lu Chieh-te, who watched the Taipei Fine Arts Museum’s galleries as a security guard, with a book published).

The year differs: Lü Pei-yi’s study puts “East Asia Lighting” and “Rainbow Paint” in 2011, while the Taiwan contemporary art database and The News Lens review give 2010 for “East Asia Lighting”; this platform uses 2010. The issue is labelled “labour and human rights”, mainly matching the temporary-worker theme of “Work History — Lu Chieh-te”.
k74.selfDesc: Lu Pei-yi's study lists Chou under 'art as an exchange platform', citing Toolkit (2010), TOA Lighting and Rainbow Paint (2011) with their 'feedback' mechanism of sponsor-donated lamps/paint turned into museum resources, and The History of Work - Lu Chieh-Te (2012), with the artist as a mediator of flowing resources. A solo-show review carried by The News Lens (by Rahma Khazam, trans. Wu Chia-ying, c.2016) notes TOA Lighting (2010) using sponsor-provided fixtures to light an empty museum space, entering the collection after the show, 'on one hand showing the mechanism of art production, on the other the fruitful collaboration between art and the economy'; The History of Work (2012) with the day-labourer Lu Chieh-Te guarding the show at TFAM.
k74.editNote: Among the ten artists in Lu Pei-yi's study. Year discrepancy: Lu groups TOA Lighting and Rainbow Paint as 2011, while the Taiwan Contemporary Art Archive and the News Lens review give TOA Lighting as 2010; the platform uses 2010, noted. The case centres on the 'exchange platform / mediator' practice with TOA Lighting as the key piece, folding in Toolkit and The History of Work. Tagged 'labour and human rights', mainly for the day-labourer theme of The History of Work and the art-economy critique. An artist's own work.
k74.pedagogicalInsight: The most borrowable thing is making “how resources flow” itself the work: the artist does not avoid mechanisms such as grants, sponsorship and collections but lays them open and lets resources flow and return within them. For courses on art, money, institutions and labour, it shows an “intermediary” position — not criticising the system from outside but entering it, operating it and then exposing it.
k74.why: Verified: Lu Pei-yi's study (academic) and the solo-show review on The News Lens corroborate TOA Lighting's sponsor-lamps-light-empty-museum-then-collection 'feedback/exchange' mechanism and the day-labourer collaboration in The History of Work. Caveat: the year is given two ways (Lu 2011; the review and the Taiwan Contemporary Art Archive 2010, the platform using 2010); Toolkit's details come mainly from Lu.

k75.name: Five Hundred Lemon Trees
k75.creator: Huang Po-chih
k75.place: Abandoned farmland replanted with lemons (Lu: three plots in Beipu, Hsinchu; Huang's own talk: the family lemon field near Guanyin)
k75.year: from 2013 (trees planted by 2015, Taipei Arts Award 2015; TFAM solo show 2016)
k75.summary:
“Five Hundred Lemon Trees” (called “Five Hundred Lemon Trees” with a different measure word in Lü Pei-yi’s study) is a long-term project by Huang Po-chih begun in 2013. He treated the museum exhibition as a mechanism, pre-selling “wine labels” to the public to raise funds, using the money to re-prepare abandoned farmland and plant lemon trees; years later the lemons would be harvested and made into lemon wine, returned to those who had bought labels.

Through a bottle of wine not yet made, the project lays out the relations of agriculture, land, economy and production and consumption; Huang’s mother had been a garment-factory worker and his family has a farming background, so the project also ties into his family’s life history.

The lemon trees were all planted by 2015, the project won the Taipei Arts Award, and in 2016 the solo show “Five Hundred Lemon Trees: Organic Archive” was held at the Taipei Fine Arts Museum. The location is given two ways: Lü’s study says three plots of abandoned farmland in Beipu, Hsinchu, while Huang’s conversation describes the family lemon field near Guanyin.
k75.selfDesc: Lu Pei-yi's study gives Five Hundred Lemon Trees (2013) using the museum exhibition as a mechanism, pre-selling wine labels, the money as seed funding to replant lemon trees on three plots of abandoned farmland in Beipu, Hsinchu, made into lemon wine two years later for the label buyers, examining agriculture, economy, livelihood consumption and production; it also mentions Production Line - Made in China & Made in Taiwan (2014) linking Shenzhen and Taipei through his mother's garment-worker life. A No Man's Land talk between Huang Po-chih and Huang Chien-yu (carried by The News Lens) notes the five hundred trees were by then all planted, labels sold to crowdfund, the ground floor of the family home converted into a small lemon-wine workshop, the project winning the 2015 Taipei Arts Award and a 2016 TFAM solo show Five Hundred Lemon Trees: Organic Archive, with the lemon field at the family home 'near Guanyin'.
k75.editNote: Among the ten artists in Lu Pei-yi's study. Title wording presented both ways (Lu writes it with one character for 'trees', the 2016 TFAM solo show with another); the place differs too: Lu says 'three plots of abandoned farmland in Beipu, Hsinchu', while Huang's talk says 'the family field near Guanyin (Taoyuan)' - both given, with 'city' set to Lu's Hsinchu for now and noted. With buyers participating and family co-production, also tagged socially engaged art.
k75.pedagogicalInsight: The most borrowable thing is using “a thing not yet finished” (wine not yet made) to open up a production chain: from fundraising, land preparation and planting to winemaking and returning the wine, participants connect themselves to a piece of land and a stretch of time by buying. For courses on agriculture, food, land and economy, it shows how to turn the abstract “producer–consumer relation” into a concrete project that takes years to harvest.
k75.why: Verified: Lu Pei-yi's study (academic) and the Huang Po-chih talk on No Man's Land (via The News Lens) corroborate Five Hundred Lemon Trees (from 2013), pre-selling wine labels to crowdfund, planting five hundred lemon trees on abandoned farmland, and brewing lemon wine for the buyers years later, with the talk adding the 2015 Taipei Arts Award and the 2016 TFAM solo show. Caveat: the planting site differs by source (Lu 'three plots in Beipu, Hsinchu'; the talk 'the family field near Guanyin'), both given; the title's 'trees' character differs.

k72.name: The Treasure Hill Tea + Photo Project
k72.creator: Wei-Li Yeh (with Yu-Hsin Wu and others)
k72.place: Treasure Hill (Gongguan settlement) artist village, Taipei
k72.summary:
The Treasure Hill Tea + Photo Project (THTP) is a long-term project by Yeh Wei-li, who moved into Taipei’s Treasure Hill settlement from 2004 (residency about 2004–2006, with the project continuing to 2008). Asking “what can an artist do in a community?”, he opened a space for tea and photography in the settlement, took portraits of residents, tidied the garden and worked with neighbours.

In contrast with active community intervention, he took a passive stance of “waiting for the visitor” — letting reality and relationships come to him, and growing work from them.

The project ran in several phases and was gathered in the final “Oversight” phase, shown at Centre A in Vancouver in 2008 with a book published. It has community interaction but remains mainly an artist-led individual project.
k72.selfDesc: Lu Pei-yi's study lists it under 'art intervening in reality', with Yeh moving into Treasure Hill in 2004, asking 'what can an artist do in a community', running a tea-and-photo space, taking portraits, tending a garden and working with neighbours in a 'waiting' posture ('reality finds you'), the final 'Oversight' phase shown in 2008 at Centre A, Vancouver. The Asia Art Archive records The Treasure Hill Tea + Photo Project / Phase Five / Oversight (2008), with Yeh's photographs and letters and Yu-Hsin Wu's video, an essay by Amy Cheng, 144 pages, in Traditional Chinese and English.
k72.editNote: Among the ten artists in Lu Pei-yi's study. The residency dates (2004-2006) and the tea-photo house, portraits, garden and 'waiting' details come from Lu; AAA independently confirms the project title, site (Treasure Hill), authors (Yeh + Wu), photo/video media and the 2008 'Phase Five Oversight' publication, showing a multi-phase project running to 2008. Tagged community art for its community contact, but mainly an artist-led personal project.
k72.pedagogicalInsight: The most borrowable thing is “passive entry”: rather than parachuting into a community with a fixed plan, first settle in, open a space for tea and photographs, let relationships happen and then grow work. For courses on community residency and place writing, it shows slowing down and building trust through everyday contact; it can also be contrasted with actively interventionist projects to discuss the pros and cons of the two stances.
k72.why: Verified: Lu Pei-yi's study (academic) and the Asia Art Archive record corroborate that THTP is Yeh's project at Treasure Hill, with photography and Yu-Hsin Wu's video and an essay by Amy Cheng. Caveat: the exact residency span (2004-2006) and the tea-photo-house, portrait and 'waiting' details come from Lu; AAA is a 2008 'Phase Five' publication showing the project ran in phases to 2008, so the year is given as 'from 2004'.

k73.name: Marshal Tie Jia - Turtle Island
k73.creator: Hsu Chia-wei
k73.place: A small island off Matsu (around Beigan); the deity Marshal Tie Jia came from Wu-Yi Mountain in China
k73.summary:
“Marshal Tie Jia – Turtle Island” is a 2012 video installation by Hsu Chia-wei. It centres on a small island off Matsu and its guardian deity “Marshal Tie Jia”, a frog god: the god originally had a temple at Wuyi Mountain in China, which was destroyed in the Cultural Revolution, and the god travelled to Matsu.

Hsu used green-screen compositing to rebuild an imagined original temple on the island, then slowly pulled the camera back to reveal the green screen, placing myth, history and memories of cross-strait migration in one frame.

The filming was done through a continuing process of asking the god’s permission and negotiating. “Turtle Island” appears in the title, while Art Basel records only “a small island off Matsu” without naming Beigan; it is the artist’s individual work, on local history and belief.
k73.selfDesc: Lu Pei-yi's study lists Marshal Tie Jia under 'art intervening in reality', built on the site's own history, telling local memory through the image, the filming done amid consulting and negotiating with the deity - a passive intervention ('reality finds you'). The Art Basel catalogue records Marshal Tie Jia - Turtle Island (2012), set on a small island off Matsu, under the protection of the local god 'Marshal Tie Jia' (a frog deity) whose temple on Wu-Yi Mountain in China was destroyed in the Cultural Revolution before migrating to Matsu, a video installation that rebuilds a fictional original temple on the island with green-screen compositing.
k73.editNote: Among the ten artists in Lu Pei-yi's study, which also mentions Hsu's The Story of Hoping Island (2008); this platform takes the year-certain Marshal Tie Jia - Turtle Island (2012), carried by both Lu and Art Basel, as the unit. 'Turtle Island' is from the work's title; Art Basel notes only 'a small island off Matsu', not Beigan, so the place is given as Matsu (Lienchiang County), with Beigan from Lu's context. An artist's own work on local history and belief.
k73.pedagogicalInsight: The most borrowable thing is making “local gods and history” the protagonist of the narrative rather than a backdrop: Hsu lets the filming itself be a process of negotiating with the god, so the work’s mode of production echoes local belief. For courses on local memory, folk belief and cross-strait migration, it shows how a concrete object / god can draw out a whole ignored history.
k73.why: Verified: Lu Pei-yi's study (academic) and the Art Basel catalogue corroborate Marshal Tie Jia - Turtle Island (2012), the small island off Matsu, the frog deity whose Wu-Yi Mountain temple was destroyed in the Cultural Revolution before migrating to Matsu, and the green-screen fictional-temple video installation. Caveat: 'Beigan' is from Lu's context (Art Basel says only 'a small island off Matsu'); the consult-the-deity filming process is from Lu.

k69.name: Factory
k69.creator: Chen Chieh-jen
k69.place: Taoyuan - the Lien Fu Garment Factory (filming site); shown in museums
k69.summary:
“Factory” is a 2003 video work by Chen Chieh-jen (about 30 min 50 sec, super 16 mm transferred to DVD, silent). He invited women workers who had worked more than twenty years at the Lien Fu garment factory in Taoyuan, and lost their jobs when management closed the factory in bad faith and refused to pay pensions and severance, to return to the factory, abandoned for about seven years, and “work”; in the film the women play themselves.

The film cuts in old black-and-white documentaries, outlining the decline of Taiwan’s export-processing industry as production moved out, to countries with cheaper labour after the factory closed.

Chen sees the filming as “creating another double” for the women and “writing people’s memory” for them, letting a struggle that seemed over continue. It is the artist’s individual work; the women returning to the site to play themselves is a collusion with the artist, not community co-creation.
k69.selfDesc: Lu Pei-yi's study lists Factory as a case of 'art revealing reality'; Chen's own statement (IT PARK) and iniva (London) name the site as the Lien Fu Garment Factory, where the women worked over twenty years before an unscrupulous closure that denied them pensions and severance, the plant left derelict about seven years before filming (c.1996); Public Delivery notes the film is 30'50", super-16mm transferred to DVD, silent, with the women re-enacting on site, the factory having reopened in a country with cheaper labour.
k69.pedagogicalInsight: The most borrowable methods are “letting the people concerned play themselves” and “returning to the site”: Chen does not speak for workers but lets the women return to the abandoned factory and re-enact, becoming the film’s doubles. For courses on labour and local industrial history, it shows how to turn abstract “industrial relocation” into concrete bodies and scenes, and warns against the crude pose of “the artist who cares about the underclass”.
k69.why: Verified: Lu Pei-yi's study (academic) and two third-party art institutions (Public Delivery, iniva) corroborate Factory (2003), the Lien Fu closed-factory women re-enacting on site, and the offshoring context. Caveat: none names the factory's county directly; Taoyuan is inferred from the Lien Fu plant being the 1996 Taoyuan Lien Fu closure case; IT PARK carries Chen's own statement (first-party) and is not counted alone as independent.

k70.name: Mirage: Disused Public Property in Taiwan
k70.creator: Yao Jui-chung + Lost Society Document (LSD)
k70.place: A nationwide sampling survey of disused public facilities ('mosquito halls'); the team is Taipei-based, with books and shows
k70.summary:
“Mirage: A Sampling Survey of Idle Public Facilities in Taiwan” is a nationwide sampling survey of idle public facilities (“mosquito halls”) carried out since 2010 by the Lost Society Documents (LSD), a group of artist Yao Jui-chung and his students; the first volume was published in 2010 and by 2018 it was in its ninth year.

Students returned to their home towns to survey and photograph with an artist’s eye; from 2010 to 2014 they surveyed over four hundred idle public facilities and published four volumes; the new book “Mirage VI” records 100 idle or under-used cases (about a third being “mosquito halls”). The outcome is archive-style black-and-white photo books of several hundred pages.

The project exposed public waste that surrounds daily life yet is ignored, drew attention from media and senior officials, and formed a civil watchdog force; Yao stepped back to be organiser / teacher and paid for it all himself to keep freedom of speech and independence of action.
k70.selfDesc: Lu Pei-yi's study gives 2010-2014, over four hundred disused facilities surveyed, four volumes published, the artist stepping back as organiser or teacher, self-funded throughout. CNA (via Storm Media, 2018-05-17) notes Yao teaches at NTNU and TNUA, leads students as 'Lost Society Document', vol.1 of Mirage published in 2010, by 2018 in its 9th year, the new Mirage VI recording 100 idle or under-used cases (about a third being 'mosquito halls'), and recalls premier Wu Den-yih's 2010 pledge to revitalise idle spaces within a year, with many still unimproved (e.g. the Hengchun visitor centre in Pingtung).
k70.editNote: Among the ten artists named in Lu Pei-yi's study. The project is a nationwide sampling with no single site; 'city' is set to the team's Taipei base for now, noted here as nationwide, and map counts are indicative only. Led by Yao with students, it is participatory, so also tagged socially engaged art. The two sources differ slightly on the title (Lu: jihua2; CNA: jihua).
k70.pedagogicalInsight: The most borrowable thing is treating “fieldwork survey + archiving” as civic action: students return home to record idle facilities, which is both image training and oversight of public policy. It shows an artist stepping back to be an organiser and giving the stage to participants; it is a good method prototype for courses on local surveying and civic issues.
k70.why: Verified: Lu Pei-yi's study (academic) and the CNA report (via Storm Media) corroborate that Mirage is Yao leading 'Lost Society Document' students in surveying Taiwan's disused public facilities, vol.1 2010, a multi-volume series that drew government attention. Caveat: the counts differ (Lu's 'over four hundred' is cumulative; CNA's '100' is one volume), different volumes/measures, presented side by side; the title wording differs slightly.

k71.name: The Ruin Image Crystal Project
k71.creator: Kao Jun-honn
k71.place: Sites across Taiwan abandoned through economic liberalisation / privatisation (Lu cites the Shulin Taiwan Bus depot)
k71.summary:
“The Ruin Image Crystal Project” (called the “Ruin Crystal Project” in Lü Pei-yi’s study) is a series of ruins projects by Kao Jun-honn begun in 2012. He enters spaces in Taiwan abandoned because of economic liberalisation and privatisation, makes charcoal wall drawings on site, then presents the change of eras through drama, photography and other forms, letting people see traces forgotten by their time.

Among them, “The Thomson Project” redraws, on the walls of the Shulin Taiwan Motor Transport bus depot left derelict by privatisation, the images of the Laonong river valley taken in 1871 by British photographer John Thomson; the location later also became an important scene in Tsai Ming-liang’s film “Stray Dogs”.

“Reception Room” (2014) is recorded as a kind of sequel to this project, set in the abandoned Xindian prison, a disused mine in Sanxia and elsewhere. It has many ruins and no single location; it is the artist’s individual work, included for its theme of ruins and privatisation.
k71.selfDesc: Lu Pei-yi's study lists The Ruins Crystal Project (2012) under 'art revealing reality', with Kao sketching on site in ruins and presenting era-change through theatre and photography; 'The Thomson Project' redraws Thomson's 1871 Laonong-valley image in charcoal at the Shulin Taiwan Bus depot, the scene becoming a location in Tsai Ming-liang's Stray Dogs. The Taiwan International Video Art Exhibition (twvideoart.org) Kao page notes Detention Center (2014) as 'a kind of sequel to The Ruin Image Crystal Project', set in an abandoned Xindian prison, Sanxia mines and so on.
k71.editNote: Among the ten artists in Lu Pei-yi's study. Lu calls it 'Ruins Crystal Project'; the common full title is The Ruin Image Crystal Project, used here. Multiple ruins, no single site; 'city' is set to Lu's cited Shulin Taiwan Bus depot (Shulin, New Taipei) and noted. Included as an artist's own project on the ruins/privatisation issue.
k71.pedagogicalInsight: The most borrowable thing is treating “ruins” as a site for reading political and economic history: not using ruins as a backdrop but entering, staying and drawing historical images on the walls so the space itself becomes teaching material. For courses on local history, urban change and industry / privatisation, it shows the approach of “the body entering the site and rewriting memory through drawing and images”.
k71.why: Pending: Lu Pei-yi's study details the 2012 Ruins Crystal Project, the Shulin Taiwan Bus 'Thomson Project' and the Stray Dogs location, all as one detailed source. The Taiwan International Video Art Exhibition page independently confirms The Ruin Image Crystal Project exists (Detention Center 2014 is its sequel) but does not corroborate the 2012 year or the Shulin/Thomson specifics, so it stays pending until a second source directly corroborates the project's year and content.

k66.name: Stroll, a Place with Light (Dalongtian Living Aesthetics 2025)
k66.creator: National Tainan University of the Arts; co-host Tainan Municipal Guantian Junior High School (a Ministry of Education 2025/114 USR project)
k66.place: Guantian District, Tainan; shown at Guantian Junior High, drawing on the Longtian night market and its night-time streets
k66.summary:
“Wandering Where the Light Is” is a Ministry of Education 2025 (ROC year 114) USR art exhibition by the Tainan National University of the Arts and Tainan Municipal Guantian Junior High School, opening on 8 November 2025 and running to 30 December, free every day 17:00–21:30, with the venue at Guantian Junior High.

The exhibition takes inspiration from Guantian’s “night-market wandering” culture, holding that the stall lights of Longtian’s night streets not only gather crowds but also carry residents’ living memories; exhibits include multimedia works such as the “Glowing Water Chestnut” by the university’s students.

The lighting at the opening was led jointly by the two schools’ principals, with a legislator and the head of the Longtian Night Market management committee attending. Residents were not co-creators but audience / participants; placing this case under “Greater Longtian Life Aesthetics to the Countryside” is inferred from the continuing 2026 show.
k66.selfDesc: Economic Daily News (2025-11-08) reports: the show was co-hosted by TNNUA and Guantian Junior High under a Ministry of Education 2025 (114) USR project, opening 11/8 and running to 12/30, 17:00–21:30 daily; the opening lighting was led by principal Chiu Shang-chia and Guantian Junior High principal Ching Shih-lung, with legislator Kuo Kuo-wen speaking and the Longtian night-market committee chair attending; a glowing water-caltrop was a TNNUA student work, and the show took Guantian’s night-market ‘stroll’ culture as its inspiration.
k66.pedagogicalInsight: The most borrowable thing is taking “the lights of night-market stalls” as the way in: everyday things residents see daily and take for granted are looked at anew as material carrying living memory. For teachers of local aesthetics or living memory, it shows how to grow a theme from students’ own life scenes rather than giving an outside topic. Note residents were not co-creators but audience / participants.
k66.why: Unverified: so far a single source, Economic Daily News (2025-11-08), corroborating the TNNUA × Guantian Junior High Ministry of Education 2025 (114) USR show ‘Stroll, a Place with Light’, its run and the glowing water-caltrops. The project name ‘Dalongtian Living Aesthetics’ and the departments and curators do not appear in this piece (they appear in the 2026 edition’s China Daily News report); grouping this edition under Dalongtian is the platform’s inference from the same school and theme, pending a second source that directly reports this 2025 edition.

k68.name: Light Light Light Longlai (Dalongtian Living Aesthetics 2026)
k68.creator: National Tainan University of the Arts (a cross-department collaboration of the Dept. of Materials Art & Design and the Dept. of Art History & Cultural Heritage); curating teachers Cheng Cheng-hsiung, Hsu Yuan-ta and Chen Ming-hung; co-host Tainan Municipal Guantian Junior High School
k68.place: Guantian District, Tainan; shown at Guantian Junior High, drawing on the Longtian night market and its night-time streets
k68.summary:
“Light Light Light Lónglái” is the 2026 annual cross-department art exhibition of the Tainan National University of the Arts’ “Greater Longtian Life Aesthetics to the Countryside” USR project, held at Guantian Junior High by the Department of Materials Creation and Design and the Department of Art History and Cultural Heritage, with the school as co-organiser; teachers Cheng Cheng-hsiung, Hsu Yuan-ta and Chen Ming-hung co-curated it, and it runs to 20 December.

The title plays on “Light” and the Taiwanese word for “come” to invite people into Longtian, continuing the theme of the lights of Longtian night market and night streets, with works that let viewers feel they are walking into a tunnel of light and shadow.

The project team also ran two paper-folding lantern-painting workshops at Guantian Junior High, with students’ works shown at the same time. For this 2026 show alone there is so far only one article (China Daily News / Yahoo) and no second independent source.
k68.selfDesc: China Daily News (2026-11-17) reports: the show is TNNUA’s annual art show run under USR with Guantian Junior High, a cross-department collaboration of the Materials Art & Design and Art History & Cultural Heritage departments, co-hosted by Guantian Junior High, curated by Cheng Cheng-hsiung, Hsu Yuan-ta and Chen Ming-hung; it is a key outcome of the ‘Dalongtian Living Aesthetics into the Countryside’ USR project, with a light-tunnel effect, two paper-lantern workshops and students’ works on show, running to 12/20.
k68.pedagogicalInsight: It continues the entry point of “night-market lights = living memory” and makes the venue an experience through a “tunnel of light and shadow”. The lantern workshops are a low-barrier participation form that can be borrowed directly, letting local students make things by hand. Note it leans toward “students make, residents view”; residents are not co-creators.
k68.why: Unverified: so far a single independent source, China Daily News (2026-11-17, with Yahoo a reprint of the same piece), corroborating the 2026 ‘Light Light Light Longlai’ of TNNUA’s ‘Dalongtian Living Aesthetics’ USR project at Guantian Junior High, the cross-department collaboration, curators and lantern workshops. It belongs to the same project as the 2025 ‘Stroll, a Place with Light’ (K66, Economic Daily News) but is a different year and exhibition; this edition alone still rests on one source, pending a second.

k67.name: Return and Take Root — Nanying Regional Image Action Project
k67.creator: College of Sound and Image Arts, National Tainan University of the Arts; project leader Tseng Chi-hsien (director of the Graduate Institute of Documentary and Film Archiving), co-led by Tsai Ching-tung, Hsieh Yu-en and Lin Chiao-fang; partners Beimen Community University and the Senao Technology Foundation
k67.place: Tainan; results show at TNNUA’s College of Sound and Image Arts (Guantian); fieldwork across Dongshan, Yujing, Qigu, Beimen and Guantian, extending to Jiangjun and Jiali
k67.summary:
The Tainan National University of the Arts’ College of Audio-Visual Arts ran the “Return and Root: Nan-ying Region Image Action Project” under the Ministry of Education USR programme, with a results exhibition on 5–6 December 2025 at the college in Guantian. The project lead is Tseng Chi-hsien, director of the Graduate Institute of Documentary and Film Archiving; partners include the Beimen Community University and the Shennao Technology Cultural and Educational Foundation.

The project spans five Tainan districts — Dongshan, Yujing, Qigu, Beimen and Guantian — with five sub-projects (“Guantian Chronicles, Yujing Image Records, Beimen Salt Study, Nan-ying Time, Dujia Film Camp”), using film reading groups, a summer film camp, a mobile photo studio, rescue of family videotapes and outdoor film-reel screenings, involving primary and junior high teachers and students, graduate students and local elders.

They record temples, the salt-belt area, mango and vanilla industries and ordinary people’s memories, building a cross-generation path of image action. The sources do not give participant numbers or the number of works for each sub-project.
k67.selfDesc: Economic Daily News (Huang Chi-ming, 2025-12-05) and Liberty Times (Yang Chin-cheng, 2025-12-05) report: TNNUA’s College of Sound and Image Arts, under a Ministry of Education USR grant, held a results show on 12/5–6 at the college, with five sub-projects ‘Guantian Chronicle, Yujing Image, Beimen Salt Study, Nanying Time, Duka Image Camp’, covering the five districts. Economic Daily names the project leader as Tseng Chi-hsien, director of the Graduate Institute of Documentary and Film Archiving; Liberty Times says it was led by provost Tsai Ching-tung with teachers Hsieh Yu-en and Lin Chiao-fang guiding graduate students. Partners include Beimen Community University and the Senao Technology Foundation.
k67.pedagogicalInsight: The most borrowable thing is treating “images” as a cross-generation tool of action, not only a form of output: rescuing family videotapes, a mobile photo studio and outdoor film-reel screenings are concrete ways to bring elders and local memory in. For teachers of media literacy or local memory, the five sub-projects show how to design different image tasks for different communities (the salt belt, mango-growing areas). Note sub-projects are led by graduate students and teachers, while elders and residents are mostly interviewees and those recorded, so depth of participation varies by case.
k67.why: Verified: Economic Daily News (Huang Chi-ming) and Liberty Times (Yang Chin-cheng) are two media and two reporters, corroborating TNNUA’s College of Sound and Image Arts Ministry of Education USR ‘Return and Take Root’ results show (12/5–6), the five sub-projects and the five districts. Caveats: the two pieces ran the same day with partly overlapping content, possibly partly from a TNNUA press release; principal Chiu Shang-chia spoke as the school, not as project leader; the sugar-railway line name differs between the two pieces; TNNUA’s own site and USR Hub are same-source and not counted as independent corroboration.

k52.why: Unverified: so far a single source, 1111 News (from the university). The material, size, participating units and supporting bodies are as the release states, which explicitly says students and community volunteers made it together; the number of volunteers, how many workshops and the completion date remain to be filled in.
k52.name: Co-created Vine Ox 'Light and Shadow' Project (vine-ox installation, Gongqi community, Dacun)
k52.creator: Lai Jian-yuan of Da-Yeh University's Dept. of Design (USR Hub 'New Life for Tradition') and Yoshida Atsushi of its Dept. of Plastic Arts; Gewei International Co.; Gongqi Community Development Association (executive secretary Lai Guo-huai)
k52.place: Children's park at the Gongqi community center, Dacun Township, Changhua County
k52.summary:
Teachers and students of Da-Yeh University’s departments of Design and Plastic Arts worked with volunteers of the Gongqi community in Dacun, Changhua, using discarded grapevines to build a rattan ox about three metres tall in the community centre’s children’s park, symbolising the resilience and innovation of farming villages.

It is part of Da-Yeh University’s USR programme (Lai Jian-yuan of Design, “Tradition Reborn”, and Yoshida Atsushi of Plastic Arts); the report is dated 28 November 2024.

The community’s general secretary described the process as facing several challenges of time and space; the project was supported by the Ministry of Culture, the Changhua Life Aesthetics Museum and the Dacun Township Office. The sources do not give the number of volunteers, workshop sessions or the completion date.
k52.selfDesc: 1111 News (from the university) reports that the roughly three-metre work was made from discarded grapevines by teachers and students of Da-Yeh University's design and plastic-arts departments together with Gongqi community volunteers, with support from the Ministry of Culture, the Changhua Living Art Center and the Dacun Township Office.
k52.pedagogicalInsight: Turning discarded grapevines into a three-metre rattan ox, made by university staff and students together with community volunteers, models building community with “local waste material + making together” for teachers working with USR or communities. Note that the issue leans toward local cohesion with little social edge, so it suits an example of “material transformation and community collaboration” rather than issue depth.

k53.why: Verified: the core facts — that Lukang Gilgle (Chang Ching-yeh) launched the This-Autumn Arts Festival from 2015 and worked with local shops and old houses — are separately reported and cross-confirmed by several independent sources including CommonWealth Magazine, Smile Taiwan and PAR (Performing Arts Review); but these are mostly profiles of the person or organization and do not pin down the full details of any one edition, so specific editions remain to be verified.
k53.name: Lukang This-Autumn Arts Festival
k53.creator: Lukang Gilgle cultural enterprise (curator Chang Ching-yeh) and the Changhua Baolu Movement Association
k53.place: Lukang Township, Changhua County (old houses, the streets and local shops)
k53.year: First edition 2015 (originally 'Lukang Arts Festival: This-Autumn Gathering'), roughly every other year since
k53.summary:
The Lukang Autumn Arts Festival is a self-funded civil arts festival launched in 2015 by returning youth Chang Ching-yeh after building community momentum through the “Save Lukang movement”; the first edition was originally called “Lukang Arts Festival: Autumn Gathering”, held roughly every other year (Commonwealth says “every two years”).

The festival works with local shops and old houses, extending exhibition space into everyday places (a family restaurant, a bar, a youth start-up base) and using neighbourhood curating, walking tours, performances, film and talks to overturn outside tourist stereotypes of Lukang.

PAR Performing Arts Magazine reports that the curators first meant it for locals, but participants were mostly from outside, while locals gradually grew used to the festival’s existence. The dates of a particular edition and whether it has continued recently are not given or lack a year in the sources.
k53.selfDesc: PAR (Performing Arts Review) reports that the curator originally meant the festival for locals, but most participants came from elsewhere while locals gradually grew used to its presence. CommonWealth Magazine and Smile Taiwan also report Chang Ching-yeh and Lukang Gilgle launching the festival in 2015 and working with local shops and old houses.
k53.pedagogicalInsight: A self-funded civil arts festival run by a returning youth and set in old houses and shops, it shows how exhibition space can extend into everyday places such as restaurants and bars. PAR notes the curators first meant it for locals but mostly outsiders came; this gap of “who is it for / who comes” is itself a topic worth discussing with students about local arts festivals.

k54.why: Verified: the core facts — that Goldfish Neighbour (Peng Ren-hong) organized the Toucheng Old Street Arts Festival from 2014 and founded a young-and-old co-creation space and the 'Young & Old Journal' — are cross-confirmed by several independent sources including PeoPo, UDN, GVM Cities and CommonWealth / Smile Taiwan; but most are interviews with the person or organization, with no complete record of any single edition, so specific editions remain to be verified.
k54.name: Goldfish Neighbour and the Toucheng Old Street Culture & Arts Festival
k54.creator: Goldfish Neighbour (founder Peng Ren-hong); visiting and international artists also take part in street-based work
k54.place: Toucheng Township, Yilan County (the old street, the former township mayor's residence)
k54.year: From 2014 (first Toucheng Old Street Arts Festival), held yearly since
k54.summary:
Peng Ren-hong, from Toucheng, returned home to work after graduate school and in 2014 applied for the Ministry of Culture’s Youth Village programme to organise the first Toucheng Old Street Art Season, which has been held each year since.

He later founded “Goldfish Neighbours”, turning the old mayor’s former residence into a youth-and-elder co-creation space, inviting elderly artists and craftspeople to be the protagonists telling their own stories, letting outside and local artists exchange, and publishing the “Youth–Silver Magazine”.

Goldfish Neighbours is a long-running place-regeneration organisation whose single “project” boundary is unclear, so it is recorded as an organisation / arts season; the Commonwealth Cities book excerpt mentions Argentine artists taking part in street-level creation, and recent editions and scale are not given in the sources.
k54.selfDesc: News Lens, PeoPo citizen journalism, a GVM Cities book excerpt, and CommonWealth / Smile Taiwan report that Peng Ren-hong, after applying to the Ministry of Culture's 2014 youth-village programme, organized the first Toucheng Old Street Arts Festival, then founded Goldfish Neighbour, ran a young-and-old co-creation space, and published the 'Young & Old Journal'.
k54.pedagogicalInsight: Peng Ren-hong turned the old mayor’s residence into a youth-and-elder co-creation space and invited elderly artists and craftspeople to tell their own stories as protagonists, modelling “elders as protagonists, not interviewees”. For those working across generations or on place regeneration, the point is to stay long-term and build community relations first, and only then talk about making.

k55.why: Verified: besides CNA (2025-01-23), United Daily News independently covered the show under a different headline, corroborating the Pingtung Indigenous Peoples Museum at Pingtung 1936, the three Paiwan artists (Hua Heng-ming and his daughters Hua Yi-ta and Hua Lu-sha) working in knives, painting and ceramics, the county Indigenous Peoples Department, the run to 4/27, and the BALILAOU (sharing the land) and Mavaliu themes; upgraded to verified. The udn page shows no byline or date, so a wire reprint cannot be fully ruled out. (Daily source expansion, 2026-11-19)
k55.name: We Are Not the Only Ones on This Land (Hua Heng-ming, Hua Yi-da and Hua Lu-sha, a father-and-daughters show)
k55.creator: Paiwan artists Hua Heng-ming and his daughters Hua Yi-da and Hua Lu-sha; co-organized with the Pingtung County Government (Indigenous Peoples Administration)
k55.place: Pingtung Indigenous Peoples Gallery, Pingtung 1936 Cultural Base, Pingtung County
k55.summary:
Three Paiwan artists — Hua Heng-ming, Hua Yi-da and Hua Lu-sha, a father and daughters — put their longing for home and freedom, and their exploration of multiple identities as selves, tribe and family, into knives, painting and pottery; the show ran in 2025 at the Pingtung Indigenous Museum in the Pingtung Tobacco 1936 Cultural Base, until 27 April.

It was jointly planned by the Pingtung County Government’s Indigenous Peoples Administration and the three artists, around family (Mavaliu), tribe and shared land (Paiwan “BALILAOU”).

The county’s indigenous affairs office explains the curatorial idea comes from the Hengchun Peninsula once being land shared by different ethnic groups, where differences and conflicts are hard to avoid when plural identities coexist. It is an individual / family exhibition without resident participation; whether the works touch a concrete social issue (such as land rights) is not given in the sources.
k55.selfDesc: CNA (2025-01-23) reports that the show was co-curated by the Pingtung County Government's Indigenous Peoples Administration and the three Paiwan artists, shown at the Pingtung Indigenous Peoples Gallery in the Pingtung 1936 Cultural Base, around the themes of family (Mavaliu), tribe and shared land (the Paiwan word 'BALILAOU').
k55.pedagogicalInsight: This is a joint exhibition by a Paiwan father and daughters without community participation, suited as material for “looking at works and talking about identity”. Students can see how the three makers put questions about home, freedom and plural identities (self / tribe / family) into knives, painting and pottery. It is work-oriented, not a participatory workshop.

k56.why: Unverified: the 2025 Falling-Mountain Wind Arts Festival 'Hey, Haikou!' is reported by several outlets (Minpao, UDN, Taiwan News, Smile Taiwan), but mostly as event publicity or county-supplied material, with weak evidence of resident participation (only sparse mentions of the 'Haikou Canteen' and old-house reworking), so it is listed as unverified. The length of the residencies and whether residents actually took part in creation remain to be filled in.
k56.name: 2025 Falling-Mountain Wind Arts Festival: Hey, Haikou!
k56.creator: Pingtung County Government; 16 artists from Taiwan, France, the US, Japan and Mexico (e.g. Yosuke Yamauchi, Yu Wen-fu, Chen Shu-yen, Liu Dong, Chang Yu-chia and others)
k56.place: Haikou Village, Checheng Township, Pingtung County (three zones — village, harbour, beach — and the Sea-view Art Museum)
k56.summary:
The 2025 Fall Wind Art Season, “Hey, Haikou!”, ran from 20 December 2025 to 1 March 2026 in Haikou Village, Checheng, Pingtung; the curation centres on the winter “falling wind” peculiar to Haikou and brings together 16 artists from Taiwan and abroad, with works spread across three zones — village, harbour and beach — and the Sea-Viewing Museum.

Artists took up residence and made work to the spaces and environment: a Japanese illustrator turned cat and dog sculptures into village figures; Yu Wen-fu rebuilt an abandoned stone house with bamboo weaving and plastic chairs; the “Haikou Canteen” had Japanese cuisine craftspeople and local residents jointly offer limited lunch boxes.

NOWnews reports 2024 as the sixth edition. How long residencies lasted, whether residents actually took part in making, and whether climate and fishing-village change were actual responses in the works are not given in the sources.
k56.selfDesc: Minpao, UDN, Taiwan News and Smile Taiwan report the 2025 Falling-Mountain Wind Arts Festival under the title 'Hey, Haikou!', gathering 16 artists from Taiwan and abroad on the Haikou beach, harbour and village and at the Sea-view Art Museum; NOWnews separately reports the 2024 edition as the sixth.
k56.pedagogicalInsight: This is a tourism-leaning landscape arts festival with limited direct reference for classroom teaching; what is more borrowable is the “Haikou Canteen”, where Japanese cuisine craftspeople and residents offered limited lunch boxes together, showing that food can be a medium of contact between visiting artists and the local community. Note most works are still artist-in-residence creation, with only scattered resident participation.

k57.why: Verified: Lin Chieh-wen (Labay Eyong)'s Dungku Asang is reported and cross-confirmed by several independent sources including The News Lens (News Lens photo feature), the Taishin Arts Award site and the Academia Sinica newsletter — the artist, the Taishin shortlisting, and weaving blankets with community women to wrap the mining mountain are consistent; the number of weavers and exhibition-date details remain to be filled in.
k57.name: Dungku Asang ('Wrapping the Mountain') (Lin Chieh-wen / Labay Eyong)
k57.creator: Lin Chieh-wen (Labay Eyong, Truku of Hongye community, Hualien) and women weavers of the community
k57.place: The Ruixin mining area around Hongye community, Wanrong Township, Hualien County
k57.year: 2021 (shortlisted for the 2020 Taishin Arts Award; the Taishin page dates it 2021/3/6–3/27)
k57.summary:
“Dungku Asang” (Wrapping the Mountain) is a work by Lin Chieh-wen (Labay Eyong), who invited tribal women to weave blankets together and drape them over the Ruixin mining area worked by Asia Cement and Taiwan Cement around Hongye Village, Wanrong, Hualien; the work was shortlisted for the 2020 Taishin Arts Award, and the Taishin page is dated 6–27 March 2021.

The work leads viewers onto the land and traditional territory to look back at the traces history left in the mountain, and brings out women’s weaving and cultural traits.

Reports say she widened weaving into a concept of healing, treating the mined mountain as a wounded body. One exhibition note lists “Wrapping the Mountain” under “Labai Iyong”, probably another Chinese rendering of Labay Eyong; details of dates and place are not fully given in the sources.
k57.selfDesc: The News Lens (News Lens photo feature), the Taishin Arts Award site and the Academia Sinica newsletter report Lin Chieh-wen draping blankets over the mining mountain and being shortlisted for the Taishin Arts Award; the Taishin page dates it 2021/3/6–3/27.
k57.pedagogicalInsight: Lin Chieh-wen invited tribal women to weave blankets together and drape them over a mined mountain, likening the mined mountain to a wounded body, modelling how collective weaving — a women’s, local craft — can respond to mining and traditional-territory issues. For teachers discussing environmental or indigenous issues, this is a high-quality example of “speaking through the community’s own craft”.

k58.why: Unverified: so far a single source, 1111 News (from NTOU). The partner units, the mayor presiding over the lighting, the lantern's provenance and the marine-debris display are as the release states; the festival's exact dates and title, and who made the marine-debris works, remain to be filled in. 'NTOU' is National Taiwan Ocean University.
k58.name: Kouhu Seaside Arts Festival (with the NTOU USR team in residence)
k58.creator: National Taiwan Ocean University (NTOU) USR team; Qinku Yajiao Cultural & Creative Association (chair Wang Yao-xin); Kouhu Township Office
k58.place: Xialun area, Kouhu Township, Yunlin County
k58.year: 2025 (after the 2025 Taiwan Lantern Festival; exact dates to be confirmed)
k58.summary:
The Chenku Yajiao Cultural and Creative Association has long promoted community building and arts education in the Xialun area of Kouhu, Yunlin. The 2025 Kouhu Coastal Art Season was held by the National Taiwan Ocean University (NTOU) USR team together with the association and the Kouhu Township Office.

The art season adopted a lantern left over from the 2025 Taoyuan Taiwan Lantern Festival, with the lighting ceremony led by the township mayor, and used an ocean-debris art display to let residents understand environmental sustainability while enjoying the lantern, echoing the ideas of reusing lanterns and reusing marine debris.

Residents came with their families, but the co-creation process is thinly described, so evidence of resident participation is weak to moderate; the exact dates and name of the art season and who made the marine-debris works are not given in the sources.
k58.selfDesc: 1111 News (from NTOU) reports that the festival was run by NTOU's USR team with the Qinku Yajiao Cultural & Creative Association and the Kouhu Township Office, adopting a lantern left from the 2025 Taoyuan Taiwan Lantern Festival, with the township mayor presiding over the lighting, and promoting marine education through marine-debris art displays.
k58.pedagogicalInsight: Adopting a lantern left over from the Taiwan Lantern Festival for a second life and combining it with a marine-debris art display lets residents grasp environmental sustainability while enjoying the lantern, showing how a “ready-made festival object” can become an environmental education medium. Note that the co-creation process is thinly described, so it is closer to a showing of results.

k59.why: Unverified: although the Wuta Elementary x National Taiwan Museum 'Tnunan' Atayal-artefacts exhibition has several reports (Liberty Times, Lianet, Yahoo from the museum) agreeing on dates and place, several appear to derive from school or museum press releases and, by the platform's rules, do not count as mutually independent; the Liberty Times page could not be opened to check the full text this time. The 30-plus artefacts, 10 elder interviews and student guides are as the reports state.
k59.name: Tnunan: Returning Through Objects, Bound Together (Wuta Elementary x NTM Nan'ao Atayal artefacts special exhibition)
k59.creator: Wuta Elementary School, Nan'ao Township, Yilan County (co-curators include teacher Wilang Mawi), the National Taiwan Museum, the Nan'ao Township Atayal Culture Hall, and the Yilan County History Museum
k59.place: 2F special-exhibition room, Atayal Culture Hall, Nan'ao Township, Yilan County
k59.summary:
“Tnunan: Returning Through Objects, Bound Together” is a special exhibition of Nan’ao Atayal artefacts by Wuta Elementary School with the National Taiwan Museum and others, opening 6 October 2026 and running to 26 February 2027 in the second-floor special exhibition room of the Atayal Cultural Hall in Nan’ao, Yilan.

After about two years of artefact research, fieldwork and elders’ oral accounts, the school followed names left in the century-old acquisition registers to reconnect over 30 Nan’ao Atayal artefacts, acquired by the National Taiwan Museum in the Japanese period, with tribal families; ten elders who had lived in the old mountain settlements were interviewed, and some went to the museum’s storeroom to identify objects.

The school also turned the results into lesson plans and teaching kits and trained students as young guides. It leans toward museum curating and cultural education, and whether it fully fits the platform’s definition of an “art form” is open to discussion; some reports’ headlines say “National Museum of Taiwan History” while the text says the National Taiwan Museum, probably a headline error that could not be confirmed.
k59.selfDesc: Liberty Times, Lianet and Yahoo (from the National Taiwan Museum) report that the exhibition, by Wuta Elementary with the National Taiwan Museum and others, shows more than 30 Nan'ao Atayal artefacts, interviewed 10 elders and trained student guides, running from 6 Oct 2026 to 26 Feb 2027.
k59.pedagogicalInsight: The school followed names in century-old acquisition registers to reconnect the museum’s artefacts with tribal families, then turned results into lesson plans, a teaching kit and student guiding — a complete example of “taking artefacts as the starting question and letting students be researchers and guides”. For teachers of local culture or indigenous education, it shows how returning artefacts can be research, identity and curriculum at once.

k60.why: Unverified: so far a single independent report, in UDN, corroborating that TNUA's College of Fine Arts held the micro art festival with the Cheng Family Historic House, Wang Yu-song's 'parent-child homecoming day' turtle-mould sand-printing, and the 1980s turtle memory at Shalun; the second link, an Accupass ticketing/registration page, does not count as a second independent source. Details such as a single host's name and the 2023 opening date remain to be filled in.
k60.name: Watershed Aesthetics Art Initiative: Gongsitian Creek Action (Gongsitian Creek Micro Art Festival)
k60.creator: College of Fine Arts, Taipei National University of the Arts (TNUA); in cooperation with the Cheng Family Historic House on Gongsitian Creek; artist Wang Yu-song (sea-turtle participatory work)
k60.place: Along Gongsitian Creek to its mouth in Tamsui District, New Taipei (Shalun Beach, Zhouzi Bay, the Cheng Family Historic House)
k60.year: USR 2020–2022; 2023 Micro Art Festival (opened 10/28), 2024 satellite show 'Sea Turtles Home 1980' (10/13)
k60.summary:
The Taipei National University of the Arts College of Fine Arts used the Gongsitian Creek basin in Tamsui as its stage, turning coastal environment issues into participatory making through the micro art festival of the “Watershed Aesthetics Art Initiation: Gongsitian Creek Action” (USR, academic years 109–111); the activity was held by the university with the Cheng Family Old House, and included a market and talks.

In 2023 three zones were set along the creek, opening on 28 October; artist Wang Yu-sung planned a “Parent-Child Sea Turtle Return Day”, where families used large and small turtle moulds to take sand rubbings on Shalun Beach, recreating turtles coming ashore.

This echoes the local memory that sea turtles appeared on Shalun Beach in the 1980s and later left after war, built structures and breakwater blocks; in 2024 it continued with the satellite exhibition “Sea Turtle Return 1980” (13 October, Zhouzi Bay). The United Daily News says only “sea turtles” without naming the species.
k60.selfDesc: UDN's report 'Tamsui's Gongsitian Creek Micro Art Festival: knowing the coast through art' says the festival, run by TNUA's College of Fine Arts with the Cheng Family Historic House, included a market and talks; Wang Yu-song hosted the parent-child homecoming day, with families printing turtle tracks in the sand at Shalun using large and small turtle moulds. The report notes turtles appeared at Shalun in the 1980s (the most recent record) and left after the coast went through war, man-made structures and wave-breakers. An Accupass event page also records the 2024 'Sea Turtles Home 1980' satellite show (10/13, Zhouzi Bay).
k60.pedagogicalInsight: Turning the local ecological memory that “sea turtles once came ashore and later vanished” into families taking sand rubbings with moulds to “recreate turtles coming ashore” shows teachers of environmental education how a concrete, hands-on bodily action can carry abstract ecological change, closer to children than talking directly about ocean pollution. Note that sand rubbing is a one-off experience, so depth is still limited.

k61.why: Verified: Hakka News (Li Tai-yuan, 2023-12-23) and PeoPo (Wang Zheng-kui, 2023-12-18) are two independent sources, both directly describing Dienguang community's 'Telling the Tale of Leigonghuo', residents performing it themselves, TNUA's center accompanying them, the Amis 'Battle of Leigonghuo' history and multilingual mother tongues as the core, and the run from 2013 to the 11th edition in 2023. Details of earlier editions and each USR year remain to be filled in.
k61.name: Leigonghuo Little-Play Festival: 'Telling the Tale of Leigonghuo' (Dienguang community, Guanshan)
k61.creator: Residents of Dienguang community performing of their own accord, the Dienguang Community Development Association; accompanied by TNUA's Center for Art and Social Practice & Continuing Education; 2023 director Chan Yi-chia (performing-arts teacher at Guanshan Junior High)
k61.place: Dienguang community (Kaadaadaan), Guanshan Township, Taitung County (about 70% Amis, 20% Hakka)
k61.year: 'Telling the Tale of Leigonghuo' from 2013 (11th edition in 2023); TNUA USR sub-project 2018–2019 and 2023–2024
k61.summary:
The Dianguang tribe (Kaadaadaan) in Guanshan, Taitung — about 70% Amis and 20% Hakka — takes as its collective memory the 1896 “Thunder Fire Battle”, in which ancestors drove off remnants of Qing troops with bamboo cannons. From 2013 residents took this story onto the terraced rice fields after harvest and developed “Playing Thunder Fire”, whose 2023 run was the 11th.

The roughly one-hour show is performed by villagers, returning youth and local schoolchildren, with bamboo cannon sound effects, interweaving Amis, Hoklo, Hakka and Mandarin without subtitles, hoping to plant seeds of the mother tongue in children; in 2023 there was a first full script, directed by Zhan Yi-jia of Guanshan Junior High.

The Taipei National University of the Arts Centre for Art and Social Practice joined as an accompanying partner through the “Thunder Fire Little Theatre Festival” USR sub-project (academic years 107–108 and 112–113), helping build the theatre structure. Independent reports centre on 2023; details of earlier editions are not given in the sources.
k61.selfDesc: Hakka News (Li Tai-yuan, 2023-12-23) reports: the little play, from 2013, grew into an hour-long terraced-field theatre, performed by villagers, returnee youth and local students, with bamboo cannons added for sound; 2023 had the first full script, directed by Guanshan Junior High's Chan Yi-chia; the dialogue mixes Amis, Hoklo, Hakka and Mandarin to revitalize mother tongues. PeoPo (Wang Zheng-kui, 2023-12-18) also reports the rice-fragrance theatre opening, with thanks to TNUA among others, in its 11th staging this year.
k61.pedagogicalInsight: This is a high-quality example of three in one: the community’s own history, its own languages and its own bodies. Residents took the tribe’s Thunder Fire Battle onto their own rice fields and performed in several languages without subtitles, letting the mother tongue pass on naturally in the act of performing. For teachers of indigenous or local education, the most borrowable thing is this informal language revival of “letting children hear elders speak the mother tongue inside a play”, which feels stronger than a language class. Taipei National University of the Arts accompanied and helped build the theatre structure rather than leading, a good model of outside resources supporting local people.

k62.why: Verified: UDN (11th edition) and China Times (2018-02-22, 5th edition) are two independent sources confirming that the Hao-Cai-Tou Arts Festival is a long-running community art event in Luzhunan with resident and artist participation. TNUA's involvement appears only in UDN's programme as 'a TNUA performance', with China Times 2018 not mentioning TNUA, and the specific USR accompaniment seen mainly on school-sourced pages; so the local festival is taken as the subject and TNUA listed as a participant.
k62.name: Hao-Cai-Tou (Good Omen) Arts Festival (Luzhunan historic compound settlement)
k62.creator: Miaoli County Traditional Settlement Culture Association (local host); participation by TNUA staff and students; 2018 chief director Li Xiao-ping, visual director Qu De-yi
k62.place: Luzhunan historic compound settlement, Toufen City, Miaoli County (about 50 three-sided courtyard houses)
k62.year: Hao-Cai-Tou Arts Festival (5th in 2018, 11th in 2024); TNUA USR sub-project 'Home in Luzhunan' 2018–2019
k62.summary:
The Luzhunan old house cluster is the last large cluster of three-sided courtyard houses (about 50) in Toufen, Miaoli, kept by chance because of the 1968 building restrictions for an industrial zone. For years the local Miaoli Traditional Settlement Culture Association has built on the “Good Fortune Arts Festival”, inviting artists to make work in the old houses; 2018 was the 5th edition and 2024 the 11th.

The festival combines folk customs such as the Lantern Festival turtle-asking, street parade and DIY radish lanterns so that art interweaves with ordinary life. In 2018 director-general Li Xiao-ping stressed “the villagers are the protagonists”, with six artist teams making 12 works that year.

Taipei National University of the Arts staff and students took part in performances during the USR “Home in Luzhunan” sub-project (academic years 107–108); the United Daily News’s programme for the 11th edition lists “Taipei National University of the Arts performance”, while the China Times 2018 report does not mention the university.
k62.selfDesc: China Times (2018-02-22), 'Li Xiao-ping gives Luzhunan an artistic face', reports the 5th 2018 festival: six artist teams made 12 works, the community preserves nearly 50 courtyard houses, and Li Xiao-ping joined for the first time as chief director, saying 'the villagers are the protagonists' (no mention of TNUA). UDN's 'Into its 11th year! … Hao-Cai-Tou festival opens on the 24th' reports the 11th edition's programme, explicitly listing a TNUA performance, radish-lantern digging, turtle-borrowing and parades, running to 2/29.
k62.pedagogicalInsight: Using “Lantern Festival customs (turtle-asking, street parade, radish lanterns)” as the festival’s skeleton lets artists’ residency work grow on ordinary people’s festivals rather than running a separate art event; for teachers working with communities it shows that “connecting art to the existing rhythm of life” mobilises residents better than inventing a festival from nothing. Li Xiao-ping’s “the villagers are the protagonists” also marks the boundary of visiting artists in a community.

k63.why: Verified: ARTouch (review by Chen Si-yu) and Commercial Times (2024-01-30) are two independent sources confirming that 'A Wanhua Walk for Ordinary People' is a city art season under the Taipei Department of Urban Development's social-housing public-art framework, curator Lin Hong-john, built on years of fieldwork linking Wanhua's labour history and local memory, with works by Tu Wei-cheng, Homeless Taiwan, Lin Wang-ting and Tsai Ming-liang. Neither source mentions TNUA or USR (TNUA attribution is only school-sourced), and the curatorial-team name (Waley Art vs Hengguan Creative) and dates differ slightly, noted in the editor's note.
k63.name: A Wanhua Walk for Ordinary People
k63.creator: Host: Taipei City Department of Urban Development (social-housing public art); curator Lin Hong-john (professor, TNUA Fine Arts Dept.); curatorial team Waley Art (director Peng Cai-xuan) / execution by Hengguan Creative; more than 20 artists including Tsai Ming-liang, Chang Chien-chi and Tu Wei-cheng
k63.place: Wanhua District, Taipei (Qingnian Phase II, Juguang and Fuxing social housing; venues include Zhongshan Hall, Bopiliao and Waley Art)
k63.summary:
“A Wanhua Stroll for Ordinary People” is a city art season held from 9 January to 25 February 2024 (opening at Zhongshan Hall on 30 January), organised by the Taipei City Urban Development Bureau under its social housing public art framework, curated by Lin Hung-chang and run by the local space Water Valley Art (the Commercial Times names the curatorial team as Hengguan Creative).

About 20 artists, drawing on several years of fieldwork, linked shops, social welfare groups and residents of social housing (Qingnian Phase 2, Juguang, Fuxing), rewriting Wanhua’s labour history and local memory through video, textiles and workshops, and giving the position of storytelling back to “ordinary people”.

Examples: Tu Wei-cheng’s object-imprinting workshop “Cabinet of Many Treasures” with residents, Mangcaoxin’s work from homeless people’s cardboard boxes “Walk and Bump into Monga”, Lin Wang-ting’s “Amber Project” recording Nanjichang relocated households, and Tsai Ming-liang’s piece on “Xining National Housing”. The tie to National Taipei University of the Arts’ USR appears only in the university’s own source; neither independent source mentions the university.
k63.selfDesc: ARTouch (review by Chen Si-yu) records the host as the Taipei Department of Urban Development, curator Lin Hong-john, team Waley Art, running 2024.01.09–02.25, noting Tu Wei-cheng's 'Cabinet of Many Trades' resident-object relief-printing workshop, Homeless Taiwan's 'Come Bump Around Monga' homeless cardboard boxes, and Lin Wang-ting's 'Amber Project' point-cloud scans of Nanjichang demolition households. Commercial Times (2024-01-30) records the 1/30 opening at Zhongshan Hall, three social-housing sites (Qingnian Phase II / Juguang / Fuxing), Tsai Ming-liang's 'Xining Public Housing', about 20 artists, and curatorial team Hengguan Creative.
k63.pedagogicalInsight: “Giving the position of storytelling back to ordinary people” is the most borrowable spirit here: artists built on several years of fieldwork so that the labour and lives of shops, welfare clients and social-housing residents became the content of works (residents bringing objects to imprint, homeless people’s cardboard boxes used to talk about space). For teachers working with communities or issues, it shows public art need not be one big piece but long-term staying that lets locals’ everyday lives be seen. Note it is a city art season under the Urban Development Bureau’s social housing public art framework, with larger scale and resources.

k64.why: Unverified: the two sources that directly name the TNUA special exhibition 'Memory on the Margins' and curator Wang Bao-xuan both belong to the National Human Rights Museum (press release + online exhibition — same institution, not mutually independent); Storm Media / The Journalist (2020-07-18) reports only the 2020 Green Island Human Rights Art Festival as a whole (21 artist groups) and does not name the TNUA special exhibition, so that part currently rests on a single institution's sources. The museum's release confirms the collaboration with TNUA, the 'memory politics and artistic intervention' course, and five student works on 'memory's periphery'; the exact supervising teachers' names do not appear in readable sources.
k64.name: Memory on the Margins — TNUA Special Exhibition at the Green Island Human Rights Art Festival
k64.creator: Teachers and students from art departments at Taipei National University of the Arts (TNUA); TNUA special-exhibition curator Wang Bao-xuan; the National Human Rights Museum (2020 Green Island Human Rights Art Festival, overall curator Luo Xiu-zhi)
k64.place: White Terror Green Island Memorial Park, National Human Rights Museum, Green Island Township, Taitung County
k64.summary:
The National Taipei University of the Arts worked with the National Human Rights Museum to embed an education-and-creation project in the 2020 Green Island Human Rights Art Festival (15 May to 15 September, at the White Terror Green Island Memorial Park).

Students of arts departments first learned the context of the White Terror and transitional justice through the course “Politics of Memory and Artistic Intervention”, then took up residence in the park and made site-specific work on “Memory Periphery / Edge”, producing 5 student works; the university’s special exhibition was curated by Wang Pao-hsuan and the festival’s overall curator was Luo Hsiu-chih.

The creators were university students, not local residents or victims’ communities; the press release says “students” made the works and does not mention teachers co-creating, and the exact name of the supervising teacher does not appear in readable sources.
k64.selfDesc: The National Human Rights Museum's press release (2020-05-15), 'The 2020 Green Island Human Rights Art Festival opens — speaking from the margins through contemporary art', records: the festival ran 5/15–9/15 at the White Terror Green Island Memorial Park; this year it worked for the first time with domestic art departments including TNUA, combining the 'memory politics and artistic intervention' course, with students producing five works themed on memory's periphery (the release mentions student creation, not teacher co-creation); the festival's overall curator was Luo Xiu-zhi. The exhibition title 'Memory on the Margins' and curator Wang Bao-xuan appear in the museum's online exhibition. Storm Media / The Journalist (Li Jia-ying, 2020-07-18) discusses the festival as a whole (21 artist groups) without naming the TNUA special exhibition.
k64.pedagogicalInsight: This is an arts-education example of “first take a course to understand the context, then make work on site”: students took “Politics of Memory and Artistic Intervention” to learn the White Terror and transitional justice, then took up residence at Green Island and turned history into works. For teachers of issues or history, it shows a full teaching arc of “knowledge building → on-site response → making”. Note the creators were university students, not local residents or victims’ communities, so it is a teaching case of “how students understand and translate others’ traumatic history”, not community co-creation.

k65.why: Verified: the core facts — that Poor People's Taipei has been run by the Poverty Solidarity alliance (Pinxuemeng) since 2017, with people experiencing poverty as creators, questioning the city's inclusiveness — are cross-confirmed by several independent sources including CNA (2024-04-26), the Museum Island newsletter (Ministry of Culture) and Right Plus (2024-06-07). Still to clarify: the year and run of the 8th edition 'Only the Shadow I'm Still Getting to Know' (the Bopiliao official page is robots-blocked and was not read); and the role of people with lived experience in curatorial decisions, which most reports do not detail. Right Plus mis-prints the run dates, noted in the editor's note, with CNA taken as authoritative.
k65.name: Poor People's Taipei (project)
k65.creator: Initiated by the Poverty Solidarity alliance (Pinxuemeng); co-planned with Do You a Flavor (Chu Kang-yung) and others; over the years, partner NGOs and people with experience of poverty (homeless people, migrant workers, those in precarious situations) as the creators
k65.place: Around Wanhua, Taipei (venues over the years include Bopiliao Historic Block, the Museum of Contemporary Art Taipei, Yima IMMA / Nanjichang, and the Little Red House Menstruation Museum)
k65.year: From 2017 (in 2024, the spring preview 'Transfer Station' at MOCA and the autumn 7th edition 'Daydreaming' at Bopiliao)
k65.summary:
“Poor People’s Taipei” is an annual project run since 2017 by the Anti-Poverty Alliance (Learning from the Poor), using exhibitions and forums to let people with experience of poverty — homeless people, migrant workers, mothers in vulnerable situations, people with mental illness and children in adversity — speak as “creators” about the Taipei they see, asking how inclusive the city is.

Over the years it has co-created with a dozen or more NGOs and artists (pottery, scent blending, painting, clay, installation, video and more), and exhibitions deliberately do not label creators’ identity or status so the works themselves stand out. In spring 2024 a pilot show “Transfer Station” (27 April–16 June, 13 artist groups) was held at the Museum of Contemporary Art Taipei, and in autumn the seventh edition “Daydream Wandering” (15 October–14 November) at Bopiliao, with satellite shows at IMMA and Little Red House.

Right Plus records this as a pilot show, the project entering its 8th year and shifting to a biennial format, with 19 partner NGOs co-creating with artists. Most reports do not detail experienced people’s role in curatorial decisions, so co-creation is mostly at the level of works; the year and dates of the eighth edition could not be verified.
