k65.selfDesc: CNA (Wang Bao-er, 2024-04-26) reports 'Transfer Station' at MOCA Taipei (4/27–6/16, 13 artist groups): Pinxuemeng is made up of people with experience of poverty, NGOs, artists and sociologists, co-planning with Do You a Flavor's Chu Kang-yung; Chang Yu-yi's 'Friendly Chair Project' uses armrest-crowded benches to show homeless people's situation, and the show deliberately does not label the creators. Right Plus (2024-06-07) records this as a preview, the project entering its 8th year and shifting to a biennial format, with 19 partner NGOs and artists co-creating (Community Empowerment Association pottery and scent, City Wanderer painting and clay, Lohas migration maps, Do You a Flavor's long installation 'What Wind Blew You Here'). The Museum Island newsletter (Ministry of Culture) records the autumn 7th edition 'Daydreaming' at Bopiliao (10/15–11/14), with satellite shows at Yima IMMA and the Little Red House, understanding poverty as material, spiritual and relational lack and exclusion.
k65.pedagogicalInsight: The most borrowable thing is that it flips people with experience of poverty from “objects displayed and labelled” into “creators”, and deliberately does not label creators’ identity or status, so the work is seen first rather than first being tagged “homeless” or “single mother”. For teachers working with disadvantaged or sensitive issues, this design of “remove the label first and let people speak as creators” is key. The co-creation methods are also varied and borrowable: pottery and scent blending, reviewing life with painting and clay, hand-drawn migration maps, and a long installation collecting voices. Note most reports do not detail experienced people’s role in curatorial decisions, so co-creation is mostly at the level of works.

k51.name: Shigang Mama Theatre
k51.creator: Shigang Mama Theatre (members are mostly Hakka and working women of Shigang, non-professional; leader Yang Chen-chen); mentored into being by Assignment Theatre (artistic director Chung Chiao); director Li Hsiu-hsun
k51.year: Founded 2000 (out of People's Theatre workshops run by Assignment Theatre in the Shigang/Dongshi quake zone after the 1999 921 earthquake); signature work 'Pear Blossom Heart-Land' was the 2021 20th-anniversary production
k51.summary:
The Shigang Mothers’ Theatre Troupe grew out of the 1999 921 earthquake: Chai-Tsih Theatre (Chung Chiao, Li Hsiu-hsun) ran people’s theatre workshops with affected women in the quake areas of Shigang and Dongshi; the mothers in the drama class did not want to disband and from 2000, with Chai-Tsih’s supportive guidance, formed a self-governed community troupe. Most members are Hakka women who came to Shigang through marriage, and for years they have made work with their own bodies from their farm and daily labour (picking pears, washing clothes, stir-frying).

The 2021 20th-anniversary work “Pear Blossom Heart” was performed by the members themselves, with a script co-written by all members and then edited by a professional director; it opened with a documentary film on the troupe’s history, then began with the labour of picking pears and washing clothes and invited the audience to plant pears in Shigang together.

The work deals with Hakka women’s position under patriarchal clan rules, rebuilding the family and self-identity. In 2023 “Meeting of a Millennium”, produced by Chai-Tsih Theatre, had the troupe on stage with local residents.
k51.selfDesc: The Performing Arts Reviews site (Hsu Jen-hao, 2021-03-17) notes that after the 1999 921 quake Assignment Theatre's Chung Chiao and Li Hsiu-hsun did psychological rebuilding in the Shigang Hakka village, and a year later the drama-class mothers, unwilling to disband, formed the troupe, with Yang Chen-chen as leader and Li Hsiu-hsun as director; it observes members mostly came through marriage and face Hakka patriarchal constraints, using labour such as pear-picking, washing, cooking and killing chickens as material, opening with a documentary and inviting the audience to plant pears. The NCAF grant archive records 'Pear Blossom Heart-Land' (Shigang Mama Theatre, submitted by Assignment Theatre) as a 2020 grant, performed 12-13 Mar 2021 at Treasure Hill, 2 shows and 144 attendances, directed by Li Hsiu-hsun with Chung Chiao shaping the script, co-written by all members, touring under the title 'Pear Blossom' since 2005. Assignment Theatre's site states it was founded 1996, ran People's Theatre workshops with quake-struck women in Dongshi and Shigang in 1999, and mentored the troupe from 2000. China Times (2023-02-22) reports 'Encounter of a Thousand Years' as Assignment Theatre's new Hakka work, with the resident-founded Shigang Mama Theatre on stage, an environmental-theatre version in Shigang in Nov 2022 and a 2023 run at the National Taichung Theater with the Hakka Affairs Council.
k51.pedagogicalInsight: This is a rare amateur community theatre in Taiwan that has lasted more than twenty years, a treasure for facilitators. The core to borrow is “starting from participants’ own bodies and labour”: everyday work such as picking pears, washing clothes and stir-frying is turned into performance material and ritual, rather than handing out a script to act. The script is co-written by all members and edited by a professional director, showing how to balance amateur autonomy and professional guidance. The opening documentary lets participants first see “who we are and how far we have come”; the ending invites the audience to plant pears in Shigang, turning them from onlookers into participants. A reminder for educators is the time scale: its depth comes from twenty years of accompaniment, not a one-off workshop. With Chai-Tsih Theatre and Li Hsiu-hsun’s professional guidance behind it, how to keep professionals from drowning out amateur voices is a question to keep asking.
k51.why: Verified: the origin (Assignment Theatre mentoring in Shigang after the 1999 921 quake, founded 2000) is consistent across The News Lens, the Performing Arts Reviews site and Assignment Theatre's own account; that the troupe is made of Shigang Hakka women, works from labour, and has long resident participation is corroborated by the Performing Arts Reviews critique, China Times and the NCAF grant archive.

k50.name: Sixteen Coming-of-Age Youth Arts Festival (series, incl. the Youth Playmaking Project)
k50.creator: Tainan City Cultural Affairs Bureau (host); Influence New Theatre (partner on the Youth Playmaking Project; artistic director Lu Yi-hsin, per 2017 reporting); supported by the Ministry of Culture and the TSMC Education and Culture Foundation
k50.place: Tainan City (2026 venues: Tainan Cultural Center, Tsang-kang Cultural Center, Wu Garden Hall and the new Tainan Public Library main branch)
k50.year: From about 2015 (inferred from edition numbers; sources do not state a start year); 2017 was the Playmaking Project's 3rd year, 2025 the 11th edition, 2026 the 12th year
k50.summary:
Tainan’s old city has the coming-of-age tradition of “doing sixteen”, which the city’s Cultural Affairs Bureau has turned into a youth arts festival each summer. It has run since about 2015 (the sources do not state the start year; it is calculated from edition numbers), and its core “Youth Stage Play Project” recruits 16- to 18-year-old vocational and senior high students who, after six months and three stages of training, collectively create and publicly perform a ticketed original play.

In 2017 (then named the “Sixteen Little Theatre Festival”) the project reached its third year, with nearly 50 students from 17 high schools creating “Kaleidoscope”; the 11th edition in 2025 (5 July–31 August, theme “Real Me”) recruited 48 participants and staged the 11th play, “Authentic”, plus a street culture month, a visual exhibition, weekend talks and an outdoor performance market.

The 12th year in 2026 (18 July–23 August, theme “Touch: the Frequency of Youth”) staged the 12th play, “Touch · Feel Seen”, recruiting youths from 16 schools across 19 districts of Tainan, Yunlin and Kaohsiung, and ran youth theatre observers and the community senior programme “Interactive GO”.
k50.selfDesc: China Times (2017-03-23) reported the Cultural Affairs Bureau's collaboration with Influence New Theatre, the 'Sixteen Little Theatre Festival – Youth Playmaking Project', in its 3rd year: from March, over half a year of three-stage training, about 50 students from 17 high schools created 'Kaleidoscope' from the Tainan coming-of-age rite, performed in August at the Tainan Cultural Center; the project combined art with life education, was led by Influence New Theatre's artistic director Lu Yi-hsin and supported by the TSMC foundation. UDN (2025) reported the 11th edition ('Real Me', 5 Jul–31 Aug): 48 recruits, the 11th play 'Authentic' (15–17 Aug, 4 shows), a cumulative 536 participants and over 40,000 attendances, limited gifts for those born Sep 2008–Aug 2009 who complete the rite, plus a July street-culture month, an August visual show, eight weekend talks and a 16–17 Aug outdoor market. UDN (2026) reported the 12th year ('Touch', 18 Jul–23 Aug), recruiting youths from 16 schools across 19 districts of Tainan, Yunlin and Kaohsiung to create the 12th play 'Feel Seen' (22–23 Aug, Tsang-kang Theatre, ticketed via OPENTIX), with youth theatre observers and a senior-community Interactive GO.
k50.pedagogicalInsight: This is a good case of turning a local coming-of-age tradition into a platform for young people’s own creation. The most borrowable part is the full arc: six months and three stages of training, youths collectively create a play from their own life experience, then really perform it publicly with tickets. It treats young people as real creators rather than as doing an exercise to hand in; “really performing for people and selling tickets” is itself strong motivation. Using “doing sixteen”, a local rite, as the theme also makes abstract “identity / growing up” concrete and tied to their own city; facilitators can start from a real ritual or milestone in students’ lives instead of asking vaguely “who are you?”. Note it is a large city-run festival with ticketing, a market and souvenirs; what belongs to arts education is the training and collective creation of the play project, while the festival’s outer layer is more city branding — students can look at the two separately.
k50.why: Verified: the festival's existence and year-on-year continuity are corroborated across different years and outlets (China Times 2017, UDN 2026). Each year's detail is largely press-release style and partly single-source (and the two 2025 pieces appear to be the same release, not independent), as noted.

k49.name: Treasure Hill 'art-and-living coexistence' settlement (series)
k49.creator: Taipei City Cultural Affairs Bureau and the Taipei Culture Foundation's Artist Village division (operation); resident artists and original residents; ceramicist Chou Ling-chih (in residence from 2008, co-designed the shared garden)
k49.place: Zhongzheng District, Taipei — the Treasure Hill settlement
k49.year: Settlement mainly 1960s–70s informal buildings (official site); registered a historic settlement in 2004, art village taken over by the foundation on 2 Oct 2010, continuing today
k49.summary:
Treasure Hill is an informal settlement built by retired veterans on a hillside in Gongguan, Taipei; it was zoned as park land in 1980 and, after residents’ petitions and pushes by academics and heritage groups, was registered as a historic settlement in 2004. The Taipei City Department of Cultural Affairs planned it as a “co-living of art and residence” settlement where households and an artist village coexist, run by the Taipei Cultural Foundation, which formally took over the Treasure Hill International Artist Village on 2 October 2010.

After artists moved in, they held shared “one dish each” meals with residents, the annual March Lantern Festival (light installations), jointly opened a shared vegetable garden and helped original residents run the “Baocun Grocery”. The official site admits that the “residence” in “co-living” first meant community residents but has since widened to units and resident artists in the settlement.

But preservation came with the dispute over residents’ 2006 relocation, the number of residents kept falling and 19 original households remain; scholars also criticise that interaction between artists and residents is “still too little” and analyse the preservation as a kind of “museumification”. The settlement was kept, but not necessarily its people.
k49.selfDesc: The official site says 'art-and-living coexistence' revitalises Treasure Hill by building art and living together, and admits that 'living' first meant the community's residents but has since widened to all the units and occupants in the settlement; the settlement is formed of 1960s–70s informal buildings, was registered as a historic settlement in 2004, repairs by the Bureau began in late 2006, and over twenty-odd years the Taipei Artist Village and Treasure Hill together have hosted more than 500 creators from over 40 countries. Fu Jen student outlet Vita (on PeoPo, 2023-11-03) records resident participation: a roughly bimonthly 'one dish per household' meal; after the March light festival residents also create in the garden, and a big bamboo cage left from an earlier festival was taken by residents to raise chickens and geese; the 'Treasure Village' shop is run by Auntie Qiuhong with the village's help, serving a set meal on Tuesdays and Thursdays; Chou Ling-chih moved in in 2008 and co-designed the shared garden; early on an elderly veteran demanded artists show a 'residence permit' and waved a cane to drive them off, tourists wandered into homes, and the village used surname signs and stanchions to protect privacy; 19 original households remain. PTS 'Our Island' (a 2007 piece, not re-read this time) is cited by the user as reporting that in 2006 some sixty-odd households moved out but only 16 actually entered transitional housing, with some residents calling it eviction in disguise. Eyes on Place (Liu Ke-chiang, 2021-01-06) notes residents keep declining, that under current rules the housing area could be empty within about a decade, that artist–resident interaction is 'still too little', and that a film-and-video experimental school occupies housing originally reserved for residents but vacated as they left. King's College London scholar Igor Rogelja analyses the preservation as a form of 'museumification': after the city offered three compensation/relocation options in 2006, it cleared the village on 22 Dec 2006 and riot police cleared the rest on 30 Jan 2007; renovated houses were let on 12-year tenancies, and households fell from over 70 before eviction to 21 in 2014 and 19 in 2018, the author arguing this turns residents and artists into a watched 'living diorama'.
k49.pedagogicalInsight: This is the best case for discussing what happens when art moves into a place where people still live and which carries historical scars; both sides must be seen. What can be borrowed is making shared life itself the method: one-dish-each meals, a shared garden and a grocery are not an event but a way for artists and residents to build relations slowly in daily life; after the Lantern Festival residents made things in the garden and used the big bamboo cages to raise chickens and geese, an example of residents taking art over into life. The more important material is its cracks: the site widened “residence” from original residents to all units, while scholars point to shrinking numbers and “still too little” interaction. Ask students: when we say “co-living”, whose “residence” is counted? Does preserving the houses mean keeping the people? Scholar Rogelja’s critique can serve as a sharper question: when preserved residents become “living dioramas” to be watched, who is preservation for?
k49.why: Verified: the core facts (an informal settlement saved as a historic settlement, the coexistence model, the three-option 2006 relocation and clearance, a fall from over 70 households to about 19, the museumification dispute) are corroborated by the official site, Rogelja's academic paper citing Taipei City documents, the 2006 Liberty Times report, the Eyes on Place scholar piece and PTS. The specific resident co-creation activities still rest on a single source, as noted.

k48.name: Daxi Daxi (series)
k48.creator: Taoyuan City Cultural Affairs Bureau and the Daxi Wood Art Ecomuseum (hosts); designer Liao Xiao-zi (key visuals for four editions); BIAS Architects (execution, book)
k48.place: Daxi District, Taoyuan — Puji Temple and the old town
k48.year: From 2018 (series; detailed content known for 2022, 2–22 Jul, and 2026, opening 18 Jul)
k48.summary:
The procession for the birthday of Lord Guan at Daxi Puji Temple (24th day of the sixth lunar month, called Daxi people’s “second New Year”) was originally a faith celebration begun by residents themselves. From 2018 the Taoyuan Daxi Wood Art Ecomuseum used museum methods to turn it into the festival brand “Daxi Daxi”, with the core idea “experience × participation × revival” and designer Liao Xiao-zi making the main visual for four editions.

The 2022 edition (2–22 July) offered the pop-up picture book “Daxi Daxi” with lesson plans and the interactive deity-generals exhibition “Wu De Dian”, and invited people to wear paper generals’ hats and join the “Parade with the Gods”; the 2026 edition (opening 18 July) centred on “festival music”, with 32 shetou groups and about 40 events, including a concert in which 9 shetou worked with pop music teams.

The festival involves the temple, volunteers, Daxi’s trades and shetou from many places; a shetou is a procession group formed by residents on the basis of shared trade or locality. The platform has read fuller material only for the 2022 and 2026 editions; other editions are not checked in detail.
k48.selfDesc: The museum's official page frames Daxi Daxi as preserving and re-presenting a 'century-old intangible cultural asset', using Daxi itself as the stage and drawing residents, shops and audiences into experiential learning; it explains the participants include temple staff, volunteers, Daxi's trades and the shetou — self-organised procession troupes formed by shared trade or locality (e.g. the ox-plough, ink-line and plasterer-boy troupes). VERSE's book panel (2023) notes Daxi Daxi has run since 2018, that BIAS Architects and the museum produced the book, and that Liao Xiao-zi designed the key visuals for four editions, calling it 'a city festival across contemporary design and folk belief'. Marie Claire (2022) records the pop-up book (Liao as art director), the 'Wu De Dian' show (with a 'righteous-steps' learning device), the 'procession with the gods' handing out paper hats, Vitali co-branded sodas, and 'Daxi Daxi' merchandise and amulets. Storm (2026) notes the bureau's 'experience, participation, revival' core and that residents, shetou and shops co-created the curation.
k48.pedagogicalInsight: This case shows how an existing local tradition can be turned into a scene that outsiders and young people can enter. The point is not what the museum invented but how design and experience devices turn onlookers into participants: paper generals’ hats walk people into the procession, the “Righteous Step” learning device lets the body understand the deity-generals, and the picture book and lesson plans help Daxi people tell their own festival as a story. What can be borrowed is to first find what the community already does, then design an “entrance for participation”; a shetou is an existing group formed by trade or locality, not an individual. Another tension to ask students about is commercialisation: do the Guan Gong co-branded soda and the “righteous bag” bring more people into the festival, or turn faith into consumption? There is no standard answer, which suits a class debate.
k48.why: Verified: the official page and three different outlets (VERSE 2023, Marie Claire 2022, Storm 2026) corroborate the hosts, the 'experience/participation/revival' idea, Liao Xiao-zi's four editions of key visuals and shetou participation. A few details (the 2018 start, 32 shetou / ~40 events) still rest on single sources, as noted.

k47.name: 2022 Mattauw Land Art Festival: A Thousand Names of the Zengwen River
k47.creator: Chief curator Gong Zhuo-jun (龔卓軍); co-curator Luo Jian-yu (羅健毓); advisers Qiu Ru-hua (丘如華) and Zeng Xu-zheng (曾旭正); hosted by the Tainan City Government Cultural Affairs Bureau (per Storm Media; the official site shows the host only as logos); nine sub-projects
k47.place: Zongye Art Center in Mattau, Tainan, plus the Dubar and Dalongtian zones (per the official site) and the Provincial Road 171 area, with partners from the upper to lower Zengwen River; sources name the zones differently
k47.summary:
The 2022 Mattauw Land Art Festival, “The Thousand Names of the Zengwen River”, is an “advocacy-type” land art festival organised by the Tainan City Government Cultural Affairs Bureau with the whole Zengwen River basin as its protagonist, running from 15 October 2022 to 29 January 2023; its venues include Magoh Sogo Art Centre, Dubao and Dalongtian (spelled differently by sources), and it is the edition before the 2026 one (K32). The official site calls it the “first nationwide” land art festival with a whole stream as its subject, with the long-term goal of “river legal personhood” and a “river-basin community” as the core of action.

The site mentions “three years of long-term field surveys”; the programme has nine units — small projects, water, bamboo, stealth photography, planting, soil, farming, sound and original projects — linking local partners from the Tsou villages upstream, the meandering rural areas midstream and the irrigation canals and fish ponds downstream.

It also ran civic participation activities such as the “Parliament of All Things” and the “Little News” news camp, plus three joint presentations. The Reporter’s “stealth photography project” feature records photographers and writers staying long-term along the basin, photographing modern Tsou hunters, mango growers, “water keepers” and youths from multicultural families.
k47.selfDesc: The official site's 'About' page calls it the 'nation's first' land art festival with a whole river as its subject, with the long-term goal of 'legal personhood for rivers' and a 'watershed community' as the core of its action and awareness; it calls on people to 'exchange bodies with bodies' and enter the living worlds of the river. It mentions 'three years of long-term fieldwork' and 'three years of research', lists nine sub-projects and three joint presentations, and says it links partners from Tsou villages upstream, meandering farm villages midstream and canal-and-fishpond areas downstream, promoting public participation and deliberation through the 'Parliament of All Things' and the 'Little News' news camp. Storm Media (2022) calls it 'Taiwan's first art festival focused on river rights', hosted by the Tainan Cultural Affairs Bureau, and says Chiayi County and the Water Resources Agency were invited to sign a watershed governance agreement (the article does not say whether it was signed). The Reporter's Sneak Photography feature records photographers and writers staying long-term along the basin, photographing a Tsou modern hunter, mango growers, 'water keepers' and young people from multicultural families.
k47.pedagogicalInsight: “A river with a thousand names” is a very usable classroom question: what is the same stream called, and how is it used, by hunters, fruit growers, water keepers and children? Take students along a canal, drain or small river to collect what people call it and their water-use stories, so the issue grows from residents’ own words. The case also models “stay first, curate later”. Note: it is an advocacy-type festival whose goal of “river legal personhood” was set from the start, so ask one more layer in class: where did this stance come from, and can students disagree? The site gives only the names of the “Parliament of All Things” and “Little News” camp, not how they were led, so check the organiser’s own method before borrowing.
k47.why: The official site (organiser's own account), Storm Media and the Reporter feature agree on the host, chief curator, run dates, zones and theme, and the Commercial Times (2023) also gives the host and chief curator; but the Reporter feature is output of one of the festival's own sub-projects and does not count as independent, and the edition numbering and level of resident participation remain unconfirmed, as noted (November 2026).

k46.name: Matsu International Art Island (ten-year ‘turning the soil’ art plan)
k46.creator: Lienchiang County Government (host); General Association of Chinese Culture (support); ‘Dapu plus+’ on Dongju (co-execution). First edition (2022) led by Wu Han-chung; third edition (2025) theme curator Nakaw Putun, with zone curators including Hung Yu-cheng, Huang Chen-yen and Kuo Mei-chun.
k46.place: The five islands of Lienchiang (Nangan, Beigan, Dongyin, Dongju, Xiju); sites include wartime strongpoints, bunkers, bomb shelters, harbours and village houses
k46.year: From 2022 (three editions held: 2022, 2023, 2025; planned by the county as a ten-year project)
k46.summary:
The Matsu International Art Island (Ten-Year Art Soil-Turning Project) is a ten-year large-scale art programme by the Lienchiang County Government; three editions have been held since 2022 (2022, 2023, 2025), across the county’s four townships and five islands (Nangan, Beigan, Dongyin, Dongju, Xiju), at front-line strongpoints, bunkers, air-raid shelters, harbour inlets and settlement houses. The Reporter notes that after wartime governance ended in 1992 the county proposed the art island as the first step of cultural governance, aiming to stabilise tourist flows, deepen cultural value and train local talent.

The programme invites artists from Taiwan and abroad to place works in Matsu’s front-line sites, settlements and maritime life, and to translate military space with local materials such as Matsu glass liquor bottles and marine debris. The first edition (2022, “Island Brewing”) had 41 teams and 39 works, with 50 Taiwanese volunteers coming to the islands for the “Island Return Bar” sub-project; the third edition (2025, “Clap Chiu — Your Sea, My Land”) had over 50 works under three themes, “Front-line Matsu”, “Islands’ Matsu” and “Ocean’s Matsu”, plus “Ten People, Ten Seas”, made by local teachers and students with residents of Ogijima in Japan.

Issues covered include regenerating strongpoints after wartime governance ended, everyday memory, revival of the Eastern Min language, population loss and the marine environment. The Reporter also notes that residents mostly see the art island as a way of bringing tourists and income and feel little about the art itself, a short publicity period made works less visible, and one student said the art island has “not yet been put into locals’ calendars”.
k46.selfDesc: The Reporter (2024-08-03) notes the county, after military rule was lifted in 1992, drew on Matsu’s Eastern Min culture, wartime culture, baimei beliefs and ecology to launch the art island as a first step in cultural governance, aiming to stabilise tourism and train local talent; it also records that residents largely see the island as a channel for tourists and income rather than for art, that the promotion window is too short, and that one student said the art island ‘has not yet entered local people’s calendar’. Rti (2022) records the first edition led by Wu Han-chung, 41 teams, 39 works, 8 curatorial projects and 50 volunteers (part of the ‘Island Return’ sub-project). Artemperor records the 2025 third edition hosted by the county and the General Association of Chinese Culture, with multiple curators and over 50 works.
k46.pedagogicalInsight: This is the case most worth discussing on “how a large arts festival relates to the local place”: look not only at the works but at the distance between the festival and residents. What can be borrowed is treating particular sites and local materials as starting points, and the cross-island co-making of “Ten People, Ten Seas”; the residents’ alienation recorded by The Reporter is equally teaching material — students can ask “who is the festival actually for?”, the counter-example to IBAE’s “start from context, not a preset theme”.
k46.why: Confirmed after your review (November 2026). Three independent outlets — The Reporter, Rti and Artemperor — agree on the host, curators, years and scale across three editions. Resident co-creation is moderately strong (there are concrete partners), but The Reporter also records residents’ distance, so both are kept.

k41.name: Chao Fangyuan: Seeing the Tidal Flats Art Festival (Ren Theatre's Fangyuan community theatre)
k41.creator: Fangyuan Township Office (host); Ren Theatre (operator, director Tsai Min-ni); Ren-ai community theatre (co-host)
k41.place: Fangyuan, Changhua (fishers’ plaza, tidal flats, mangrove sea-sky walk, Putian Temple)
k41.year: 2026 edition (Jul 26–Aug 1); the community theatre was formed in 2023
k41.summary:
Chaofangyuan | Seeing the Tidal Flats Art Festival is a community theatre and arts festival by Ren Theatre in Fangyuan Township, Changhua County (Fishermen’s Plaza, the intertidal zone, the mangrove sea-and-sky boardwalk and Pu Tian Temple); the 2026 edition ran from 26 July to 1 August, and the community theatre was founded in 2023. Ren Theatre’s director Tsai Min-ni proposed the “Seeing the Tidal Flats” incubation project in 2022 and in 2023 founded the community theatre with the Fangyuan Ren’ai Community Development Association.

They began with field walks, then used collective improvisation with a dozen or so local amateurs in Fangyuan (including a 90-year-old elder and junior-high students) to co-create the script, turning fishing-village life, fishing songs and oral memories into a play performed on the mud flats and intertidal zone, completing “Fangyuan, Our Hometown”. Tsai says, “collective improvisation is my working method”. A free drama class once had too few sign-ups, and the association’s chairman widened recruitment.

It has grown year by year: in June 2024 “Podou Arts Festival in Fangyuan”, in October joining the Changhua Theatre Arts Festival and moving to the Yuanlin Performing Arts Hall, and in 2025 (the third year) expanding into an arts festival answered by local Fangyuan groups and linked to government resources. The 2026 edition presented four series (Tidal Settlement, Tidal Theatre, Tidal Market, Tidal Images), themed on fishing-village cultural memory and coexistence with the tidal-flat environment, with a 40-table “tide banquet” of over 400 people and a Fangyuan Junior High lion-dance drum troupe opening.
k41.selfDesc: A 2025 feature by The Reporter says Tsai met documentary director Ke Chin-yuan in 2021, proposed the plan in 2022, and in 2023 formed the community theatre, completing Fangyuan, Our Home; she calls collective improvisation her working method, and the performers are a dozen locals of widely varying ages. A free drama class was expanded when sign-ups fell short. United Daily News (2026) reports the 2026 edition’s four series, a ‘tide banquet’ of 40 tables and 400+ guests, and that Ren Theatre has taken part for four years running.
k41.pedagogicalInsight: This is one of the fullest cases of “amateurs making theatre”: the facilitator does not teach acting but uses collective improvisation so residents turn their fishing-village life, fishing songs and oral memories into a play. Note: the free drama class once had too few sign-ups and recruitment was widened — a reminder that recruitment is itself part of a participatory project.
k41.why: Confirmed as verified at your request (November 2026) on the strength of The Reporter’s independent feature plus United Daily News: the former confirms how the community theatre formed and who performed, the latter the scale of this edition.

k42.name: 2026 South-Link Art Festival: Flow of Mountain Trails
k42.creator: Taitung County Government (host); Dagedan Sea Travel (planning); curator Osan Karo; artists LUA RIVERA, basakanlan (Hsieh Cheng-yi), Wang Kuan-tung, Chen Sheng-chih
k42.place: Along the South-Link route in Daren, Jinfeng and Taimali, Taitung (Huayuan Elementary, Jialan, Jinlun Station, Laliba co-creation base and other communities)
k42.summary:
The 2026 South Link Art Festival “Flow of the Mountain Path” takes place along Daren, Jinfeng and Taimali in Taitung County (villages and sites including Huayuan Elementary School, Jialan, Jinlun Station and the Lalipa co-creation base); a City Study summary gives the exhibition period as 1 July to 31 October. The festival takes the river basin as its concept.

Four groups of artists were invited to survey the South Link landscape through residencies and live with local communities, each in residence for at least 12 days, bringing in Indigenous, Hoklo, Hakka and foreign perspectives through field collection. Works are spread across a primary school, a railway station and a co-creation base: LUA RIVERA (Mexico)’s “Elder” at Huayuan Elementary, basakanlan Hsieh Cheng-yi’s “Resilience of Life”, Wang Kuan-tung’s “Circle of Symbiosis” at Jinlun Station and Chen Sheng-chih’s “Hope · Wings” at Lalipa; Wang did Paiwan field research during his residency and put its elements into his work.

The festival also has walking tours, workshops and satellite sites such as lodgings and dining tables, and launched a limited “Wave Picnic Box” with local businesses.
k42.selfDesc: City.gvm (Global Views) reports each artist spent at least 12 days in residence, gathering fieldwork and living with residents across Indigenous, Hoklo, Hakka and foreign perspectives; Wang Kuan-tung did Paiwan fieldwork for his work. The festival also offered a limited ‘wave picnic box’ with local businesses.
k42.pedagogicalInsight: Artists worked through residencies of at least 12 days, field collection and living with residents, modelling a residency ethic of “live there first, then make”. Note: residents were mostly people being researched and lived alongside, and the real degree of co-creation is not described; with a clear tourism-promotion element, students can also discuss the line between an arts festival and tourism.
k42.why: Verified: City.gvm/Global Views (2026-08-22) and the Taitung County Government official page independently corroborate the core facts — the watershed concept, the four artists (LUA RIVERA, basakanlan/Hsieh Cheng-yi, Wang Kuan-tung, Chen Sheng-chih) and their four works and sites (THE ELDER at Huayuan Elementary, THE RESILIENCE OF LIFE at Jialan, COEXISTENCE CIRCLE at Jinlun Station, HOPE TAKES WING at Laliba), the run 1 Jul–31 Oct 2026, and the organiser (Taitung County Government) — so it is upgraded to verified. The planning team 'Dagedan Hailu' and curator Osan Karo still appear only in the original (unreadable) Hub News report, and residents actual role in creation is not detailed in any source. (daily source expansion, 2026-11-16)

k43.name: CTBC New Stage Arts Festival Charity Show: Puppet Theatre by Rural Schools
k43.creator: CTBC Cultural Foundation; Puppet & Its Double Theater (artistic director Cheng Chia-yin); teachers and students in Yilan and Gongliao (New Taipei)
k43.place: Yilan (Neicheng, Lize, Dongxing schools) and Gongliao, New Taipei (Gongliao Experimental Junior High); charity show at CTBC Financial Park, Taipei
k43.summary:
The CTBC New Stage Arts Festival charity show, “Dreamers’ Wish Fulfilment Project”, was an outdoor performance on 12 September 2026 at the CTBC Financial Park in Taipei; U-Theatre has long gone to remote areas to train seed teachers and guide students in making puppet theatre, and this year’s winning schools included Lize Elementary, Dongxing Elementary and Neicheng Junior High and Elementary in Yilan and Gongliao Experimental Junior High in New Taipei.

Students of Neicheng Junior High and Elementary in Yilan took the village’s big tree god, the Earth God and water resources as their theme and devised “The Wrongly Granted Wish” — a story about over-wishing, animals left without water and a little tree god finally growing; Gongliao Experimental Junior High took the Tanlan Historic Trail as its theme.

The charity show opened with a large puppet production co-made by U-Theatre and Japanese puppeteer Nori SAWA, combined with stories devised by teachers and students from remote areas.
k43.selfDesc: United Daily News (2026-09-14, Ho Ting-chao) says the show opened with a large puppet work co-produced by Puppet & Its Double and Japanese puppeteer Nori SAWA and combined stories by rural teachers and students; the winning schools included Lize, Dongxing and Neicheng in Yilan and Gongliao Experimental in New Taipei. The name ‘Dream Builder project’ appears in only one of the reports.
k43.pedagogicalInsight: A typical “seed teachers + student creation” model: the company does not perform for children but trains teachers and guides students to turn local beliefs (the tree god, the Earth God) and water-resource problems into their own puppet theatre. For teachers in remote or local-focused courses it shows using puppetry to let students handle an abstract ecological issue (over-wishing as water imbalance). Note: this is a corporate charity show, so the presentation carries corporate-image and performance pressure unlike the freedom of an everyday classroom.
k43.why: Verified: the two original reports were from the same media group (UDN) and not independent; on 2026-11-19 two further sources independent of each other and of UDN were found — Liberty Times / art.ltn.com.tw (Tung Po-ting, 2026-09-14) and Commercial Times (Wang Tzu-ya, 2026-09-28) — both confirming the core facts: the CTBC Cultural Foundation's New Stage Arts Festival outdoor charity show on 2026-09-12 at CTBC Financial Park, with Puppet & Its Double leading teachers and students from four rural schools (Gongliao Experimental in New Taipei; Lize, Dongxing and Neicheng schools in Yilan) in co-created puppet plays; upgraded to verified. The headline puppet musical is named 'Play On! Good Earth Band' in the two independent reports (UDN's 'co-produced with Nori SAWA' framing stays single-source); the Neicheng play title 'The Mis-wished Wish' and the Gongliao theme (this entry's summary says the Tamsui-Kavalan Trail, but Liberty Times says Gongliao 'terraced paddies') remain to be checked. (Daily source expansion, 2026-11-19)

k44.name: Making the Village Together: Zhongxing New Village Co-scene Action
k44.creator: Changhua County Cultural Affairs Bureau (host); sound artist Wu Hsiu-ming, artist Hsu Chia-chen, with the Muzhiyan team
k44.place: Zhongxing New Village (juan-cun) cultural park, Changhua
k44.summary:
“Everyone Makes a Village: Zhongxing Village Shared-Scenery Action” is a public participation programme run by the Changhua County Cultural Affairs Bureau for the public art installation at the Zhongxing Village military dependents’ village cultural park; the exhibition runs from 2 to 31 May 2026, with art actions on 2, 3, 9 and 10 May.

It arranges a series of hands-on actions: sound collection and card-game workshops, timber-frame building, parent-child interactive theatre, VR creation and photography.

The aim is to turn a formerly closed dependents’ village site into an open public space and let outsiders and residents rediscover its living memories together. The sources give dates, workshop types, artists and organisers, but not actual participant numbers or results.
k44.selfDesc: The source gives dates, workshop types, artists and host, but no attendance figures or outcomes.
k44.pedagogicalInsight: Opening a formerly closed dependents’ village site as a public space through hands-on activities such as sound collection, card games and timber-frame building is a common heritage-regeneration strategy of “opening up through participation”; it splits one site into several low-barrier entrances (sound, games, timber, VR), worth a look for teachers of local culture. Note in particular: the source is a county advertorial that the platform could not read directly, the activities are as planned, and actual participation and results have no independent corroboration, so discount it when using it as a teaching reference.
k44.why: Beyond the county-government advertorial (a CNA message-platform submission the platform originally could not read), two separately bylined reports from different outlets — Storm Media (Wang Hsiu-ho, 2026-05-01) and Yam News / GuanMedia Changhua (Chen Ya-fang, 2026-05-01) — now corroborate the host (Changhua Cultural Affairs Bureau), the artists (Wu Hsiu-ming's sound workshop, Hsu Chia-chen's card-game workshop, the Muzhiyan timber build) and the dates. But both quote the Bureau heavily and use county/Bureau-supplied images, sharing the same source as the original advertorial, so they are not independent corroboration and it stays to-be-verified. Attendance, whether former village residents co-created, and whether outcomes survive are still unsourced. (Daily source expansion, 2026-11-17)

k45.name: 2026 Second Village Opens: Art, Dance, Memory — Echoes of the Unreturned
k45.creator: Yunlin County Government (host); TAMtamARTTAIWAN (planning); BIAU Dance Theatre (Barefoot Learning series); Huwei Jianguo Village Regeneration Association (operation)
k45.place: Jianguo military-dependents’ village, Huwei, Yunlin (Villages 1 and 2; bomb shelters, sentry posts, water towers and other military remains)
k45.year: 2026 (opens Oct 31, runs to Nov 1; originally Oct 24, postponed by a typhoon)
k45.summary:
“2026 Opening the Doors of Village Two | Art · Dance · Memory: Echoes Unreturned” is an arts event at the Jianguo military dependents’ village (Villages One and Two) in Huwei Township, Yunlin County, opening on 31 October 2026 and running to 1 November; it was originally set for 24 October but postponed by a typhoon.

An arts team and an international curator placed works in the village’s military remains — air-raid shelters, sentry posts and a water tower — combined with dance workshops, talks and village tours.

It lets the village’s memory be seen through contemporary art; the event also promotes the food-and-agriculture and environmental education direction of Jianguo Village Two. The report mentions “local participation” but does not say how residents took part in curating or creating.
k45.selfDesc: The Epoch Times report gives the curatorial team, sites, content and dates, and mentions ‘local participation’ but does not say how residents took part in curating or creating.
k45.pedagogicalInsight: Placing contemporary artworks directly in military remains such as air-raid shelters, sentry posts and a water tower is a heritage-regeneration method of “using the site itself as the gallery”, letting village memory be experienced through space rather than wall labels. For teachers of local history it models “letting the historical site speak”. Note: the source mentions “local participation” but not how residents took part, so the degree of co-creation is unclear and it leans toward curation.
k45.why: Verified: beyond the user-supplied Epoch Times report (which the platform could not read directly), two independent bylined reports now corroborate the core facts — China Daily News (reporter Chen Cheng-fen, Yunlin, with her own on-site photos, 2026-10-31) and Taiwan News Net via Mediashi (reporter Li Wan-yu, 2026-10-31) — confirming the Yunlin County Government as host, the Jianguo Village Regeneration Association as operator, TAMtamARTTAIWAN as planner, BIAU Dance Theatre's 'Barefoot Learning', works set into the Villages 1-2 bomb shelters, sentry posts and water towers, and the Oct 31 and Nov 1 run; Taiwan News Net also confirms the original Oct 24 date was postponed by a typhoon. China Daily News is first-hand on-site reporting, so this is upgraded to verified. Whether residents co-created and the scale of participation are unstated in all three sources. (Daily source expansion, 2026-11-17)

k40.name: Prototype Paradise
k40.creator: Prototype Paradise; lead artist Yoyo Kung; long-term collaborator Hsiao Yu-chin (per the Taitung County Government event page)
k40.place: Huannan Market, Taipei (2023) and the grounds of Taitung Art Museum (2023); the group's base is not stated in the reports
k40.year: From 2012 (began operating in 2012; the projects this platform could read date from 2015, 2023 and 2026)
k40.summary:
Prototype Paradise is a contemporary performance group that began formally operating in 2012, with “interacting with reality” at its core, placing performance into real spaces; its works are often based on interviews. The projects this platform can read date from 2015, 2023 and 2026, and the 2023 locations include Taipei’s Huannan Market and the Taitung Art Museum grounds.

The group invites people who do not work in the arts to be “everyday-life experts”; rather than “drawing material”, the team describes what it does as more like “disturbing”. Its protagonists have included stall holders, sanitation workers, front-line museum staff and migrant workers (see the sub-projects below on the case page).

A C-LAB interview (by Hou Po-yen, 2022-11-10) notes that “everyday-life expert” is a term coined by Rimini Protokoll for amateurs who are neither professional artists nor real performers; as the creators, the team must take particular care not to disrupt sanitation workers’ work and bear the communication costs and support measures needed to ensure everything proceeds with informed consent.
k40.selfDesc: A C-LAB interview (written by Hou Po-yen, 2022-11-10) says "experts of everyday life" is a term coined by Rimini Protokoll for laypeople who are neither professional artists nor real performers; as the creative party the group must take care not to disturb sanitation workers' work and invest in communication and safeguards so that everything happens with informed consent.

subs.n: Revisit Taitung Art Museum with Your Ears
subs.t: Two sessions on October 22, 2023 (10:30–11:30, 13:30–14:30) in the grounds of Taitung Art Museum, organised by Taitung County Government; instructors Yoyo Kung and Hsiao Yu-chin, co-creating teachers Yang Hui-ju and Chang Ling-yu, and 21 students. Graduates or students of Taitung Baosang Junior High served as "voice collectors", leading audiences around the grounds to hear their interviews with the museum's front-line staff; free, capped at 20 sign-ups. (From the Taitung County Government event page; the gap between 21 students and the cap of 20 is not explained.)

subs.n: Hundred Trades Scroll: Nightingales of Huannan
subs.t: One of four invited teams in "Huannan Table: 365 Days of Market Seasons" (May 20–Aug 6, 2023, Huannan Market; commissioned by Taipei's Market Administration Office and Department of Cultural Affairs, planned and run by the Chung Tai Foundation). After months of fieldwork and close interviews, the group explored vendors' subconscious images in fragmented sleep and turned their confessions into close-whisper sound theatre. (From Artemperor and CTWANT, which read alike and quote no vendors; the "18 months on site" refers to all four teams, while for Prototype Paradise only "months" is stated.)

subs.n: Following the Garbage Truck Around Taipei
subs.t: The group went out with sanitation workers along their routes, staging street performances and interactions, with a "story minibus" segment where veteran workers shared their experience. (From the C-LAB interview; routes, dates and partners could not be confirmed.)

subs.n: Walking Through Her Everyday Life: A Migrant Worker Dog-walking Sound Story
subs.t: Listed in the performance programme of the 2026 Taoyuan Iron Rose Art Festival, March 11–16, 2026, 19:00–21:00. (The festival page gives no venue, price, creative team, funders or description; the group's own site could not be read, so interview numbers, method and any later shows are not included.)

k40.pedagogicalInsight: The group spans the whole spectrum: in Taitung, teenagers act as “collectors of voices” and interview people themselves (facilitator-led), while in Huannan Night Birds the artist edits stall holders’ confessions into sound theatre (artist-led). For educators, the most useful idea is the “everyday-life expert” stance: invite non-artists as experts in some field rather than as amateurs. Informed consent and not disrupting people’s work are also essential ethics for participatory projects.
k40.why: Verified: beyond the C-LAB interview, the international Institute for Public Art's case study independently documents Prototype Paradise's 'Travelling Around Taipei with Garbage Trucks' (2015), corroborating a curatorial team whose method combines performance, theatre, installation and public participation; PAR performing-arts magazine also carries Gong You-ying's writing on amateur participation. The group's existence and participatory method thus have two or more independent sources. Individual sub-projects vary in sourcing (the Taitung case is an organiser activity page, the Huannan case's two reports look like the same release, and the 2026 Taoyuan item gives only show times), as noted.

k38.name: Headwind Project (Chengcheng Junior High School)
k38.creator: Promoted by the Taiwan Good Foundation; supported by the Ministry of Education and Ministry of Justice; partners: Party Theatre troupe (drama) and Cloud Gate Dance School (martial arts and everyday movement); photo exhibition curator and photographer Lu Te-chen
k38.place: Chengcheng Junior High School, Hsinchu (a juvenile correctional school); the 2018 photo exhibition was at Zhongshan Underground Bookstreet, Taipei (Eslite R79)
k38.year: From 2017 (photo exhibition in Taipei from July 12, 2018; the Taiwan Good Foundation page gives Jul 12–30 without a year)
k38.summary:
The Against the Wind Project has been promoted by the Taiwan Good Foundation since 2017 at Cheng Cheng Junior High School in Hsinchu, a juvenile correctional school, bringing art into the school.

Some Act Theatre led interactive drama games, collecting stories from the youths’ own life experience and writing plays together; the Cloud Gate dance classroom led martial arts and everyday movement to practise focus, endurance and bodily expression; and a class of youths, led by curator Lu De-zhen, spent about ten months recording themselves and each other on camera. There were 15 students each in the drama and martial-arts groups, and 30 youths in the photography class.

The results were presented in a photo exhibition from 12 July 2018 (to 30 July) at the Zhongshan Underground Book Street (Eslite R79) in Taipei, with three themes: “Body Portraits”, “Film Diaries” shot by the youths themselves, and “Dance Theatre” documenting the drama and dance workshops.
k38.selfDesc: CNA (2018-07-12) reports 15 students each in the drama and martial arts groups and a 30-boy class for the photo exhibition, co-organised by the Taiwan Good Foundation and Eslite. The foundation's page lists three exhibition themes: "Body Portraits", "Film Diaries" shot by the boys themselves, and "Dance Theatre" documenting the drama and dance workshops. The Initium (2018-11-03) calls Chengcheng the first juvenile correctional school in Taiwan to practise rehabilitative education and describes dance, drama and photography with dance showings and drama rehearsals.
k38.pedagogicalInsight: In a correctional school, drama, martial arts and photography run in parallel: the drama is written from the youths’ own life stories and the photography is shot by the youths themselves, giving “atypical” students the lead in making — the most valuable lesson from this case. Note: the youths are minors in custody, so presentation of results needs special protection of personal data.
k38.why: Confirmed as verified at your request (November 2026). CNA and The Initium are independent news reports that agree on the Taiwan Good Foundation, the drama troupe, Cloud Gate's school and Chengcheng; the foundation's own page adds exhibition detail. The 2017 start rests on CNA alone for now.

k39.name: "Hearing the Voices of Along the River" Atypical Education Exhibition, National Palace Museum at Chengcheng Junior High School
k39.creator: National Palace Museum and the Agency of Corrections, Ministry of Justice (co-organisers); Chengcheng Junior High School (host/implementer); supporting: Heart Breakthrough Career Exploration Association and 104 Hope Foundation (per Commercial Times; the Epoch Times mentions only the former); art teachers not named
k39.place: Auditorium, 3rd floor of the administration building, Chengcheng Junior High School, Hsinchu County
k39.summary:
“Hearing the Sound of Along the River” is the National Palace Museum’s atypical education exhibition, held from 20 to 29 December 2019 in the auditorium on the 3rd floor of the administration building of Cheng Cheng Junior High School in Hsinchu County. Since the 1990s the Museum has served inmates with touring exhibitions, since 2010 has worked with correctional institutions on replica displays, and since 2012 on art courses and training young inmates as guides.

This time the Museum’s education team worked with the school’s Chinese, mathematics, auto repair and computer vocational teachers to bring Along the River During the Qingming Festival (Qing court version) into teaching; and from Su Shi’s Calligraphy on the Cold Food Observance poem in Huangzhou it linked to students’ life experience and extended to contemporary rap rhymes, with students writing their own lyrics and music. Preparation took nearly nine months of teaching students the relevant skills.

The venue had replicas of Palace Museum objects, VR and film, and works by students in pastel, comics, Zentangle, LINE stickers, sculpture, mechanical making and music and lyrics; students also served as guides. The youths’ full names and faces are not shown, and they express themselves through music, spoken words and text.
k39.selfDesc: The reports rely on the museum's statements and quote no students or teachers. The Commercial Times says the museum has trained juvenile inmates as guides since 2012; the Epoch Times says the museum has worked with seven correctional institutions including Taipei Prison since 2010 and does not mention 2012, so they may not describe the same thing.
k39.pedagogicalInsight: Taking Palace Museum objects (Along the River, the Cold Food poem) as a starting point and letting correctional-school students reinterpret them in pastel, comics, stickers and other media, and even act as guides, shows “a low-barrier, approachable design built on high-barrier classics”. Note: the reports read like press releases and do not describe how students took part in making.
k39.why: Two outlets agree on dates, venue, the partnership and the content, but the pieces read like one press release with no teacher or student quotes; the "since 2012" claim appears only in the Commercial Times and differs from the Epoch Times' 2010.

k37.name: Yijia Art Museum (series)
k37.creator: Graduate Institute of Arts and Humanities Education team, Taipei National University of the Arts; partner: Taipei Honor Home for Veterans; course instructor and curator Wu Dai-rong (the page does not say whether the university is the organizer)
k37.place: Taipei Honor Home for Veterans (the Home of Righteous Soldiers); creation and exhibition take place in the residents' living space
k37.year: 2019 (the team entered the site in 2014 and a 2022 GPI review calls it eight years of interaction; since 2016 the project has used the name Yijia Art Museum, with a half-day show each International Museum Day; the 2019 show was on May 18)
k37.summary:
Yi Jia Art Hall is a project in which a team from Taipei National University of the Arts has, since 2014, entered the Taipei Veterans Home (the home of the Korean War anti-communist “righteous soldiers”) and lived alongside them over the long term; from 2016 it has used the name “Yi Jia Art Hall”, turning the soldiers’ living space into a place for making and showing work, with a half-day exhibition each year on International Museum Day. The project website says the idea is to turn the home into an artistic ecomuseum, focusing on the co-creation process rather than finished works, and run alongside an elective course.

2019 marked 65 years since the soldiers came to Taiwan. The curatorial team reorganised the family-history room and took a line from a yellowed document — “How to become a completely free person within 180 days!” — as its theme; resident artists and teachers used “art-narrative practice” to explore how freedom is represented and interpreted and invited participants to think together, going back to the historical documents in the family-history room to ask how the word “freedom” is defined and used.

In 2019 it was presented in a half-day exhibition on 18 May. A 2022 book review on the Government Publications Network says the soldiers moved from outside spectators to participants in the co-creation, thinking about freedom, nation and home, trauma and views of life and death with themselves as subjects; during the pandemic the planned in-person exhibition was moved online.
k37.selfDesc: The project website says the idea is to turn the home into an artistic eco-museum that values the process of making together over finished works, paired with an elective course. In 2019 the curatorial team reorganised the history room around a sentence on yellowed documents, "How to become a completely free person within 180 days!"; resident artists and teachers explored how freedom is represented and interpreted and invited participants to think together. The GPI review (Tseng Yi on Wu Dai-rong's book) adds that Wu developed an artist-teacher residency programme encouraging students to make site-specific work; participants include students, artist-teachers, and the veteran residents and administrative staff of the home; it describes the veterans as empowering themselves through art and becoming the creators.
k37.pedagogicalInsight: This project treats the teaching process itself as the creative work, and is especially useful for teachers running long workshops. A facilitator can ask: did my questions emerge from participants’ lives, or did I preset the answers? Note: how much say the soldiers had in individual works is not described, so the actual degree of co-creation remains to be checked.
k37.why: Confirmed as verified after your review (November 2026). On Nov 3, 2026 a GPI review was added as a third source; it agrees with the team sites on the 2014 start, the International Museum Day shows and the partnership with the home, but it reviews the project leader's own book, so its independence is limited, and there is still no detail on individual veterans' participation.

k36.name: Pan-Austronesian Art Festival (Kaohsiung Museum of Fine Arts, 2021 Summer Exhibition)
k36.creator: Organized by Kaohsiung Museum of Fine Arts; director Lee Yu-ling as chief curator; New Zealand curatorial advisors Zara Stanhope and Reuben Friend; 23 artists and teams from Taiwan, Australia, New Zealand, Korea, Japan, Pakistan and France; architect Lu Chien-ming for the outdoor park
k36.place: Galleries of Kaohsiung Museum of Fine Arts, extending to the outdoor park around Neiwei Pond
k36.year: 2021 (Jul 17–Oct 31 per the museum's press release; overseas show in Washington, D.C., May 7–Jun 26, 2022)
k36.summary:
The Pan-Austronesia Art Festival was the Kaohsiung Museum of Fine Arts’ 2021 summer exhibition, running from 17 July to 31 October according to the museum’s press release, with an overseas show in Washington, D.C. from 7 May to 26 June 2022. The exhibition extends from the galleries into an outdoor park around the Neiwei pond, where a water-system plant ecology restoration is under way.

The museum turned the show into an international arts festival centred on sea and islands, inviting more than twenty groups of artists to deal with the migration of Austronesian peoples, cultural collisions in the Age of Discovery, the traces left by colonisation and resource extraction, and encounters, collisions and reconciliation between islands. The curatorial team began planning in 2019; its three themes — “From the Known to the Unknown”, “Dark Islands” and “Life Flows On” — correspond to encounter, collision and reconciliation, and the director stressed avoiding a diversity of only “noise” without “harmony”.

The outdoor park takes drift plants as its target with an “organic landscape” concept, and architect Lu Chien-ming led students of the Indigenous special class to tidy the park and restore plant ecology. Some participating artists represented Taiwan at the Taiwan Pavilion of the Yogyakarta Biennale; in 2022 four groups of Taiwanese artists also went to Washington for “Fluid Borders”.
k36.selfDesc: An interview on The News Lens says the three themes From the Known to the Unknown, Dark Islands and Cycles of Life correspond to encounter, collision and reconciliation, and the director stresses avoiding diversity with only "noise" and no "harmony". The curators began planning in 2019. The outdoor park takes drift-sea plants as its subject with an "organic landscape" concept; architect Lu Chien-ming led students of the Indigenous programme to tidy the park and restore plant diversity. Some artists (Laha Mebow, Chang Chih-chung, Jason Chiu and Margot Guillemot) represented Taiwan at the Jogja Biennale; four Taiwanese artists showed "Fluid Boundaries" in Washington in 2022.
k36.pedagogicalInsight: This is large-museum curation with very weak community participation; the more useful part for educators is its thematic framework — using three sub-themes of encounter, collision and reconciliation to discuss Austronesian migration and colonisation — which can be borrowed to organise a lesson on Austronesian culture. Note: curation-led, not participatory.
k36.why: Verified: five sources agree on the organiser, chief curator Li Yu-lin, the 23 artist groups and the theme, and the museum's own opening release confirms the 17 Jul-31 Oct 2021 run and 62 works from 7 countries. Independent criticism is still thin, but the core facts are corroborated across the organiser's release and several reports.

k35.name: Interwoven Stories (Sadiljapan Old House, Tuban)
k35.creator: Curator tjuai (Chu Lien-hui); curatorial team not named in the report
k35.place: Sadiljapan old house, Tuban Village, Daren Township
k35.year: 2026 (reported Oct 29, "from today"; end date not mentioned)
k35.summary:
The “Interwoven Stories” exhibition is held in the old house Sadiljapan in Tuban Village, Daren Township, from 1 October to 15 November 2026 (as provided by the user); a report on 29 October says it is on show “from now”.

The exhibition centres on old objects collected in the old house, including things left by a mother and utensils the family used every day; the curator starts from the household collection to explore the objects’ history and family stories, letting the objects bring out the stories of Paiwan families and the village.

The curator also discussed cultural contexts such as craft, dress and ritual, helping people of different generations learn about past life. The opening day included a tea gathering, guided tours and performances, and visitors shared how the stories moved them.
k35.selfDesc: The report says the exhibits include things left by a mother and tools the family used daily; the curator starts from the household collection to explore the objects' history and family stories, extending to Paiwan craft, clothing, rituals and history, so that people of different generations can learn about past life.
k35.pedagogicalInsight: Using “things left by a mother and utensils of everyday family life” in an old house as exhibits lets the objects tell Paiwan family stories themselves; telling stories through objects suits schools well, since one old thing can open a lesson in family history. Note: whether residents took part in curating is not reported, so it leans toward curation.
k35.why: Only one source (TITV), with promotional wording; awaiting your review. (Daily expansion, 2026-11-16: searched again for a second independent source but found only a different TITV exhibition and general Tuban travel/culture coverage — none corroborating this 'Interwoven Stories' Sadiljapan old-house show — so it stays pending with no source added.)

k32.name: 2026 Mattauw Land Art Festival: Meandering Zengwen River — the Inner Foothills
k32.creator: Chief curator Huang Ching-ying; 37 artists and teams from Taiwan, Japan, the Netherlands and elsewhere (41 works); source credited to Tainan City Government Cultural Affairs Bureau
k32.place: Seven zones: Zuoying Art Center in Madou (main venue), Zengwen Reservoir, Balin in Guantian, Paozailiao in Liujia, Zuozhen Old Street, Zhaoxing and Mizhi in Nanxi
k32.summary:
The 2026 Mattauw Land Art Festival, “Meandering Sway: The Shallow Hills of the Zengwen River”, runs from 5 September to 6 December 2026 across seven zones including the Magoh Sogo Art Centre (main venue), Zengwen Reservoir, Guantian Balin, Liujia Paozailiao, Zuozhen Old Street, and Nanxi Zhaoxing and Mizhi. Officials call it Taiwan’s first land art festival to take a single river’s whole basin as its protagonist with action advocacy at its core.

The festival takes the Zengwen River’s highly winding course as its image and focuses on the shallow-hill settlements of the middle and upper reaches. Preparation took three years, and nearly half the art projects went directly into the hill settlements: artists took up residence in settlements such as Paozailiao and Zhaoxing, doing fieldwork and interviews over three years, and invited “river-basin guides” to lead the way. For example, singer Hsieh Ming-yu created the song “Yong Yong Ah Huo” with local women of Paozailiao in Liujia after long fieldwork and accompaniment; Tsou hunter Basuya Yagumeng led Yu Hsin-lan and the Flying Squirrel Girls’ team in a flying-squirrel survey.

The festival also raises public issues such as water resources and the “river-basin sacrifice system”, a “rights of nature” advocacy, and plans an experimental “nature court”.
k32.selfDesc: The reports say preparation took three years and nearly half of the art projects went directly into foothill settlements. For example, singer Hsieh Ming-yu wrote the song "Yong-yong-a Huo" with local women of Paozailiao after long fieldwork and companionship, and Tsou hunter Basuya Agumang led Yu Hsin-lan and the Flying Squirrel Girls team on a flying squirrel survey. The festival raises "rights of nature" advocacy and the "river-basin sacrifice system" and plans an experimental "Nature Court"; it is described as Taiwan's first land art festival centred on a whole river basin and driven by advocacy.
k32.pedagogicalInsight: The festival shows the depth of co-creation that is only possible when artists spend three years in place, and its “river-basin guide” design is a good way to let local people be the guides. Note: how residents took part in most sub-projects is not described in detail.
k32.why: Four reports broadly agree on dates, zones, artist count and curators (one is a CNA wire report, one covers the Tainan City Government press conference), but all cover an official event with no independent review, the work count differs (41 vs 42) and the organizer is labelled inconsistently; awaiting your review.

k33.name: Art Heritage Community Story Co-creation: Elder Dance, Hakka Daily Life
k33.creator: Promoted by Hsinchu Living Aesthetics Center; Taichung-based Chi-Chih Physical Dance Company; residents of Douhuan Community, Toufen, Miaoli
k33.place: Presentation at the Tongluo Tea Factory of Taiwan Agriculture and Forestry Co., a Ministry of Culture "Top 100 Cultural Bases"; community: Douhuan, Toufen
k33.summary:
Dancing Together, Daily Life in a Hakka Village is a 2026 (ROC year 115) project under the National Hsinchu Living Arts Center’s “Art Domain Inheritance — Community Story Co-creation Programme”, taking plant dyeing craft and Hakka life culture in Douhuan Community, Toufen, as its subject.

The project began with exchange interviews and story collection, then used art workshops to let Douhuan residents and professional dancers (Extreme Physical Dance Company, founded in 1997) work together, turning family daily life, Hakka village life, plant-dyed works and community memories into a dance piece.

The results were presented on 4 September at the Tongluo Tea Factory of Taiwan Agriculture and Forestry Co., one of the Ministry of Culture’s “100 Cultural Bases”, with residents and dancers performing on the same stage; the Center says it will keep promoting the programme.
k33.selfDesc: The report says the project is the 2026 edition of the "Art Heritage Community Story Co-creation Project" by Hsinchu Living Aesthetics Center, taking community plant-dyeing craft and Hakka life as material and weaving plant-dyed works, family daily life and community memory into the choreography; the dance company was founded in 1997. The center says it will continue the project.
k33.pedagogicalInsight: Collecting stories through interviews first, then putting residents and professional dancers on the same stage to turn family daily life and plant dyeing into dance, handles Hakka village life through the body — better suited than words to residents who are not used to speaking about themselves. Note: the number and ages of residents and whether they took part in decisions are not reported.
k33.why: Only the Hakka News (2026-09-07) source, which reads like a press release; awaiting your review. A 2026-11-15 search for additional independent coverage found none; held as pending. (daily source expansion, 2026-11-15)

k34.name: Meeting Places: Artist-in-Residence Co-creation (Taitung)
k34.creator: Organised by the Taitung County Cultural Affairs Dept. and Taitung Art Museum; local executing teams; resident artists and local venues across the years; project observer/critic Lu Pei-yi
k34.place: Local cultural venues and arts sites across Taitung (Chenggong, Zhiben, Changbin, Tjuwabar, Dawu, etc.)
k34.year: From 2021 (2021 Return: Rhythm of the Land; 2022 Return: Rhythm of the Sea; 2023 Re-Return; 2024 How to Bond; 2026 Undercurrent)
k34.summary:
“Encountering Places · Co-creation Residency” is an artist residency and co-creation programme promoted by the Taitung County Government Cultural Affairs Department / Taitung Art Museum since 2021, carried out at local venues and cultural sites across Taitung County (Chenggong, Zhiben, Changbin, Tuban, Dawu and others). Unlike ordinary residencies that take artists out of their usual environment, it stresses artists, local venues, residents and the environment meeting and co-creating as “mutual subjects”, using the process to survey local spaces, channel resources and train local art administrators.

Each year has had a different theme: 2021 “Return: Rhythm of the Land”, 2022 “Return: Rhythm of the Sea”, 2023 “Return Again: Rethinking Landscape” (Tsai Kun-lin’s sound-installation exhibition “Voices of Many” at the Chenggong Indigenous Artefacts Museum is one result of that year), and 2024 “How to Entangle” (venues in the county could apply, and three teams were matched for two-month residencies in Tuban, Changbin and Zhiben).

2026 is “Undercurrent”, as in Juan Chung-kai’s “Veranda” in Dawu. The three 2024 residencies were recorded by the programme’s observer in the ARTouch column “Southern Potential”.
k34.selfDesc: An ARTouch Southern-Potential column by Lu Pei-yi (2024-12-06), writing as the project's observer, records the three 2024 'How to Bond' teams (Lai Yu-feng / Zhiben; Luo Yu-chi / Changbin; Chen Yu-chen & Li Pei-lun / Tjuwabar) and traces the 2021-2024 artists and venues; it invokes Wu Mali's 2006 'Tropic of Cancer Environmental Art Action' idea that 'artists become residents, residents become artists', explaining the programme's mutual-subject, process-over-product stance. Official pages of the Cultural Affairs Dept. and Taitung Art Museum, a book-launch page, Liang'an Haobao (2026 'Undercurrent'), and pages by the East Taiwan Research Association and Tjuwabar Time corroborate each year's residencies and showcases.
k34.pedagogicalInsight: The programme is itself a methodology of “mutual-subject co-creation”: it deliberately differs from the traditional residency that takes artists out of their environment, and treats local venues as bridges between artists and place. Note: the degree of “co-creation” varies by year and team, so when using the word, check who is actually making.
k34.why: Verified: the whole 'Meeting Places: Artist-in-Residence Co-creation' programme (Taitung, from 2021) is corroborated across several independent sources — Lu Pei-yi's ARTouch column (2024-12-06, independent observation/critique), Liang'an Haobao (2026 'Undercurrent') and Storm Media (2023 'Voices of Chenggong') — plus official pages of the Cultural Affairs Dept. and partner bodies. The single 2023 'Voices of Chenggong' show still rests on Storm Media plus the official page; 2024 'How to Bond' and 2026 'Undercurrent' rest on that year's sources. The Art Map piece is marked a Taitung County Government advertisement and is not counted as independent corroboration.

k01.name: Opening Gangshan: Boxes of Memory (Exhibition 2.0)
k01.creator: USR project team, College of Management, National Sun Yat-sen University; in cooperation with the Kaohsiung Museum of History
k01.place: Gangshan District (exhibited at the Kaohsiung Museum of History)
k01.summary:
This is a community art project in Gangshan, Kaohsiung, run by the USR team of the College of Management at National Sun Yat-sen University together with the Kaohsiung Museum of History.

The team invited Gangshan residents to start from their own memories and each make a “memory box”.

In 2023, 75 boxes were shown at the Kaohsiung Museum of History together with footage of the making process.
k01.selfDesc: The report says the project team and local residents made the boxes together, students inventoried the cultural resources of the old street, and elementary school teachers and pupils were among the creators. The exhibition also gave background on workshops about exploring the old street and discussing its future.
k01.pedagogicalInsight: This project shows how to turn the abstract theme of ‘local memory’ into a task anyone can do by hand; the techniques below can go straight into a classroom. Note: residents’ say over the wider curation is not reported, so the depth of co-creation is unconfirmed.
k01.why: Verified: besides the 1111 report on the 2.0 (2023) opening, Yam/今傳媒 (2022-06-16) reported the earlier 1.0 edition, corroborating residents making 'memory boxes' from their life stories and the Sun Yat-sen University-led co-creation method; the 1.0 co-organisers differ from the 2.0 (which involved the Museum of History), as noted.

k02.name: Ripples of Memory (Kaohsiung Gas Explosion Memorial Installation)
k02.creator: Artist Yen Ming-hung and team; organized by the Kaohsiung City Government Bureau of Cultural Affairs
k02.place: Intersection of Sanduo 2nd Road and Kaixuan 2nd Road (next to Wuquan Elementary School)
k02.summary:
“Ripples of Memory” is a public art installation commemorating the Kaohsiung 81 gas explosion, located at the intersection of Sanduo 2nd Road and Kaixuan 2nd Road beside Wuquan Elementary School; the project ran from 2016 to 2018.

The work uses twisted metal pipes and a broken road surface to represent the event, and sets “memory objects” provided by residents into the ground. The selection process included community forums, briefings and in-depth interviews with residents, and residents’ views were built into the jury’s priorities.

Sixteen workshops were also held, with nearly 1,000 students from nearby schools taking part. The work opened to the public in early July 2018.
k02.selfDesc: The report says the selection process included community forums, briefings and in-depth interviews with residents, and residents' opinions were weighed in the jury's evaluation. Sixteen workshops were also held, with nearly 1,000 students from nearby schools. The work opened to the public in early July 2018.
k02.pedagogicalInsight: This case shows how residents’ “memory objects” can be set into an artist-led memorial so that a community leaves personal traces in a public commemoration; the techniques below can be taken into a classroom. Note: how much was resident participation and how much artist-led is not reported.
k02.why: Verified: besides Storm Media, ARTouch (Hung Wei-che, 2018-07-09) describes this 'Ripples of Memory' land-art work in detail - the team Yen Ming-hung + Huang Ming-wei Architects, its five parts (Echo of Time, Walking Memory, Ripples, Pavement Landscape, and the participatory 'Overlap Box'), a prism refracting two rainbows daily 9:30-11:30 onto a memorial poem and the names of the 32 victims, and the choice of Wuquan Elementary (a forward command post after the blast); corroborated with Storm, it is upgraded to verified.

k03.name: Big Nose Youth · Dalinpu Memory Transit Project
k03.creator: Big Nose Youth (a local youth team; founder Cheng Tzu-ying)
k03.summary:
Dalinpu is facing relocation in 2027. A team of third-generation local young people, “Dabi Youth” (which grew out of the “Flowing Dalinpu” project by Zheng Ciying, a student at NSYSU’s arts management graduate institute), uses art and community participation to preserve the settlement’s memory.

Its core project, “Dalinpu Relocation: Memory Transfer Project”, is supported by the Ministry of Education’s Youth Community Participation Action 2.0. Members act as “cultural luggage handlers”, collecting old photos, interviewing residents and riding a “transfer bicycle” around temple courtyards. The team also ran a community workshop in which residents turned past protest banners into screen prints.

The results include the publication Winds of Dalinpu, a Dalinpu voice map and a themed exhibition that strengthen community identity; the team also records the place in short social-media videos.
k03.selfDesc: The report describes the team turning protest symbols into works of local memory, with residents taking part in the silkscreen printing. The background it gives includes disputes over industrial pollution and the relocation policy.
k03.pedagogicalInsight: The approach here is to give a role first, reach out actively, then preserve memory in a structured way — well suited to relocation, urban renewal or any place that is disappearing. Note: the timing and size of the screen-printing workshop are not reported.
k03.why: Verified: besides PTS (2025) on the community workshop turning protest banners into silkscreen prints, the Liberty Times (2026-11-08) reported the 'Big Nose Youth' memory-relay project in Dalinpu, corroborating the team and its pre-relocation memory-preservation work; the silkscreen workshop detail rests on PTS.

k04.name: Good Times Podcast (Dalinpu)
k04.creator: Hsu Jung-hung, Wu Yu-mei (a teacher at Fenglin Junior High School) and students
k04.summary:
“Rose Time” is a podcast made by students of Fenglin Junior High School in Dalinpu with their teacher, documenting Dalinpu’s food, beliefs and daily life.

The teacher guided students to interview the village chief and elders, write scripts and draw a community map, and then record the programme.
